label: The Cave
take: For her the Allegory of the Cave holds the whole teaching of awakening in one image, and Plato gives it as his answer to what paideia is. She reads the cave as a tomb and also as a womb: leaving it is a birth, with conception, gestation, labour and a midwife. In her reading the prisoners are chained by legs and neck but their hands are free, meaning free will and the heart can never be enslaved. The root cave is not society or even the body but the way an unknowing mind binds itself, and the freed must go back down out of love and justice.
more: The Cave is her favourite allegory because it condenses the whole path of liberation, and Socrates gives it as the definition of παιδεία. She reads every detail as a symbol: bound legs mean no movement and so no life, the bound neck a blocked link between mind and heart, the free hands free will. The cave is also the brain, its fire the inner cinema of vision, and it is both womb and tomb, so leaving it is death and second birth. Its exit is not a place: 'you are the gate', and the freed one must return to see the One in every form.

For her the Cave (Republic VII, 514a, third after the Sun and the Divided Line) holds the whole Hellenic path of awakening: if all else were lost, we would still have the path. Its forgotten ending is the key: the freed one must go back down, out of compassion, to understand, celebrate and raise the sensible world to its highest beauty, so the cave is a place to transfigure, not a prison to flee. She reads it on three levels (political, inner, mystical); finally the cave is a function of consciousness.

label: Paideia
take: Paideia is not diplomas, rote learning (παπαγαλία) or technical training but the art of turning the whole eye of the soul from outside to inside, from becoming toward being and the Good. She ties the word to παῖς, the child: it is all for the child, the awakening of the sacred child, the eternal being one already is. In society it is the gate that joins the citizen to the polity, which is why every power has wanted to control it. She reads modern Greek resignation partly as the result of paideia being stripped away.
more: The Cave is Plato's answer to the question 'what is paideia?', and the Sun simile shows its method: as the sun activates sight already in the eye, education activates the knowledge already within, so do not stuff children with information. Paideia and politics are 'the two Ps', life's two gates, and changing paideia is the root way to change a constitution. The educator's first task is to light the light within and shine it on others.

Παιδεία in her teaching is not the Ministry of Education's school system but spiritual education, a way of awakening and of εὐδαιμονία. Socrates defines it in the Republic as μεταστροφή, the turning of the soul from phenomena toward truth, light and being. In the Pythagoras lesson it has four stages, and in the 28 October talk it is the only soil in which a political change can take root.

label: Turning of the soul
take: Μεταστροφή is the turn from looking outward to looking inward. You will never find the exit of the cave in the senses or in space and time, where you only bang on the wall and go deeper; you must turn all your attention within. She reads the pandemic as the world forcing this turn on everyone, and the 28 October talk opens by turning attention from a remembered past to the now. What usually sets it off is being fed up with the torment of change.
more: Μεταστροφή, the turning around of the soul's eye, is for her Plato's definition of paideia (Republic 518d): the whole soul turns from phenomena and becoming toward being and the Good. Because the visible world is an inverted reflection in the mirror of becoming, the turn is a literal reversal of attention from outside to inside. She treats it as the practical heart of philosophy, and as the remedy that slowly dries the passions.

Since the sun never sets and only we turn, awakening is a turn of vision rather than a change in the world. Consciousness, like a searchlight, lives whatever it is turned toward.

label: Ever-living fire
take: Reading Heraclitus B30, she holds that the whole cosmos, intelligible, psychic and material, is an ever-living fire that no god or human made, so maker and made are one. This fire is not candle flame or electricity, which are only its reflections in the cave, but Logos, primordial consciousness, which the Platonists call Nous. It is 'kindled in measures and quenched in measures' not like a radiator switched on and off but as manifesting and unmanifest at the same moment, like the frames of a film. In Part B she extends it: justice itself is the finest, fastest fire running through everything.
more: Fire is the nature of the true self: she derives δαίμων partly from δαίω, 'to be aflame', so at your core you are a flame of pure truth, a fiery focal point (ἑστία). Hestia's ever-living fire meeting the river's water produces the soul's exhalation, and Heraclitus' wisest, dry soul raises its 'scent' to incandescence. She also derives αὔρα from a root meaning 'to kindle' (her etymology, flagged uncertain).

Fire and light run through her etymologies: philo- as fire igniting the inner fire, φ in φιλία as light that envelops, σοφία as inner light, phenomena as flashes of light within the mind. The daimon comes from burning, a local flame of Heraclitus's ever-living fire, and being set on fire is a stated purpose of philosophy; the soul is that fire cooled. In Plato's image the Good is the Sun.

label: The Good
take: The Good is the first sun, the μέγιστον μάθημα, without which no other learning counts as true knowledge. It is beyond knowledge and truth, so it is touched and lived rather than understood; its light is truth and its heat is eros. In her vocabulary the small word εὖ names this inner light: whatever is joined to it takes on goodness, and diving to one's core one finds that one's being is the Good. Following Plotinus she says that when you know it you recognise it as yourself, and it comes 'like one who never left'.
more: In the Sun simile the Good is the sun of the intelligible: it emits the light of truth, activates the nous to see, and makes ideas intelligible. Like the sun, which is the source of light without being light, the Good is the source of truth and knowledge without being either: a spring is not water. It is unknowable, so awakening is uniting with it, not knowing it; after the return to the cave she says all is the Good, even darkness.

The Good is the first principle and first cause, to which all causes trace back, and the sun outside the cave. She distinguishes it even from essence: οὐσία is unified pure consciousness without subject or object, while the Sun of the Good is the source, beyond consciousness. Yet the cave is not elsewhere: it is the Good's 'underground', differing by depth or vibration. Our entelechy is to attune our existence to it.

label: Eudaimonia
take: Eudaimonia is the final cause of all causes: behind every car, marriage or job lies the wish for it, and nothing lies behind it (Aristotle). She defines it as an unshakeable fullness and freedom that depends on no condition, and as recognising your inner fiery δαίμων, which separates it from εὐτυχία, luck that turns with chance's wheel. Security, goods and relationships are conditions for cultivating it, never its source; it comes only from the soul's inward turning, and the awakened work for the εὐδαιμονία of all beings.
more: Eudaimonia is a stable fullness that does not ride fortune's wheel: it holds 'come rain or snow' because it rests on our own nature, not on anything external. She sets it against εὐτυχία, good luck, which rises and falls with τύχη; her image is Odysseus tied to his mast. It is also political, since for Aristotle the lawgiver aims at the eudaimonia of the whole city. Recognising one's true nature as fire and as the Good is itself freedom and eudaimonia, which Pythagoras named 'the best'.

Not good luck or passing happiness: εὖ is the divine pure nature, the Good, and δαίμων the inner spirit, so eudaimonia is the inner flame touching its own source. It is lasting, unwavering wholeness that arises only from self-knowledge and never from possessions or circumstances. With Aristotle she calls it the goal of all goals and the inner programme of human nature, and she faults modern education for leaving it out.

label: Heraclitus
take: People call him 'the dark', but she calls him the most luminous philosopher she has met, one you need a 'Delian diver' to reach. She builds whole talks on his fragments: B30 on the ever-living fire, B52 on Aion as a child playing, B118 on the dry soul, the common Logos (ξυνός), and Dionysus and Hades being the same. For her he teaches a radical non-dualism in which the poet and the poem are one.
more: Heraclitus gives her the river of becoming ('everything flows') into which the soul is plunged, truth as flow rather than a fixed banner, and the dry soul as wisest. Above all she returns to his Aeon as a child playing dice: life as divine play, the dice as the One's possibilities that sensation helps bring into actuality. His 'all is one' answers where we could go to find the One.

Heraclitus appears in every talk. His fragment 50, 'it is wise to agree that all things are one', is for her the first principle of Hellenism. His logos is one and common (κοινὸς λόγος) while sleepers think they own a private mind, and his ever-living fire is what the touch of truth kindles. In the Ares lesson she cites him on mortals and immortals living each other's death.

label: Plato
take: Plato is her main source, read as an initiatory teacher of awakening rather than a builder of abstract systems. She treats the Republic, subtitled 'On the Just', as so complete that if it alone survived it would carry the quintessence of Hellenic philosophy, and its three similes (Sun, Line, Cave) as a staged map of ascent. She also draws on the Phaedo (philosophy as practice of dying), the Symposium (Diotima), the Theaetetus (maieutics), the Timaeus, the Phaedrus and above all the Cratylus for etymologies.
more: Plato is the backbone of her teaching: the Republic (which she calls the Bible of Hellenism) and its Cave, the Timaeus on soul and sensation, the Symposium's Diotima. She rejects the dualist Plato who scorns the senses and reads him as a holistic teacher of awakening whose Academy taught philosophy as a path of freedom and science until Justinian's edict. Reading the Euthyphro at 14 felt to her like remembering, Plato's own ἀνάμνησις.

Plato is her main text. The Republic gives the Cave, παιδεία as turning, the three parts of the soul and the city-soul mirroring; the Phaedo the practice of death and 'make music'; the Symposium Diotima; the Timaeus a Greek theory of the soul's seats in the body; the Cratylus her ἀρετή etymology. She adds his third category between being and non-being: becoming, the zone that 'is and is not' where the soul stirs and turns.

label: Eros
take: Eros, with wonder, is the beginning of philosophy and of all change: to love freedom, true life, the εὖ ζῆν. She derives it from ῥέω, to flow: a cosmic current that passes through you and makes you lose the old false self, which is exactly the point. In the Sun simile eros is the heat of the Good as truth is its light, so the real philosopher is incandescent rather than coldly detached, and the first trait Socrates asks of a philosopher-leader is to be ἐρωτικός. It cannot be engineered with 'five tips'; it is the mystery of the Good, and she separates it sharply from attachment and obsession.
more: She links ἔρως to εἴρω, to join and fit together (also the root of εἰρήνη, peace), and to ἐρῶ, 'I say', so eros, logos and peace belong together. Cosmically eros is the weft of universal harmony, the glue that keeps the world and our true nature from perishing. It is the strongest power in the universe and a double-edged knife: its quality shapes our health, relationships, self-knowledge and even our society. Greek philosophy does not renounce it but asks us to know it from within and steer it with the divine nous toward its natural goal.

Eros is not mere bodily attraction but the soul's impetus (ὁρμή) toward union, a rushing flow that carries us from loving one person to loving the city and the cosmos. Philosophy begins as Eros for truth, being passionately and ontologically in love with the Good. Even questioning is erotic in her reading: the eros of the question leads to the all of the answer.

label: Living well
take: Starting from Alexander, who owed ζῆν to his parents and εὖ ζῆν to Aristotle, she defines living well as one's relationship with oneself, not success, money or fame. It means freedom, virtue, inner peace (γαλήνη, ἀταραξία) and care for the common good, and it is a feast to celebrate rather than a life to endure. Paradoxically she calls it the easy path: what is hard is being tossed up and down by every honk and setback. Collective εὖ ζῆν is also the purpose of justice and what the just leader serves.

label: Justice
take: Justice is not 'getting my rights' or punishment but balance held from the middle of Themis's scale, a collective state that brings things back to the mean. Inwardly it is τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πράττειν, each part of the soul doing its own around the one fiery Self, so it is an energy and a state rather than an act. Beyond the cave, in her reading of the Cratylus, justice is the finest, fastest fire passing through all things, the self-regulation of the cosmic fire that keeps the universe balanced. With eros it is one of the two keys to the Good, and it is why the freed must return to the cave.
more: Far more than a political institution, justice for Plato and his successors is the virtue of virtues, the union of all virtues, or the state of awakening and pure beholding. It unites the divisible and the indivisible, finding the sacred mean of Heraclitus's 'one-all'. Geometrically it is the harmony of all levels, which is why she calls φ its magic key and ties the Line's five to five as the Pythagorean rhythm of justice.

The Republic, as she presents it, starts from defining justice and ends by defining everything: soul, polis, afterlife, music and education. When asked to define justice, Socrates would first ask what use the definition has in life. Her chosen line from Plato makes justice the condition of wisdom: knowledge severed from justice and the other virtues is mere cunning.

label: Nous
take: In this talk she uses νοῦς as a near synonym of consciousness and says it can work in five ways, which together make up Plato's theory of knowledge. Her central claim is that there is one wonder-worker, one prisoner, one light and one awakening, and all of them are the nous. With Marcus Aurelius she adds that all people are siblings, children of the same nous.
more: Nous is the first emanation of the One: cosmic consciousness and wisdom, the Platonic name for Heraclitus' fire and Logos. It is fluid and unified rather than a thing, and it 'cools' into soul to play the game of matter, so the body is the vehicle of the soul and the soul the vehicle of nous. True self-knowledge means recognising this fiery nous that wears the soul; her best modern Greek word for it is συνειδητότητα, awareness. Yet she also stresses that what finally awakens is beyond mind, and in her Nativity reading Joseph is the doubting mind.

Nous is not the calculating mind (λογιστικόν), which is only a sub-function; it is awareness itself, whoever perceives your thoughts, the charioteer. It is the true perceiver behind every sense ('mind sees and mind hears', to which she adds 'mind smells, mind tastes'), the soul's core, symbolised by the Circle of the Same. In her reading of myth, infant Zeus nursed by Amalthea is our nous being fed so that it remembers itself.

label: Logos
take: Logos has many meanings she draws out with her audience (cause, ratio, speech, analogy, promise, reckoning), and every vibration of spacetime is a logos, a ratio shaping the energy of the whole. With Heraclitus she insists the Logos is one and common (ξυνός, with upsilon, not ξινός, 'sour'), though most people think they have a private understanding. The fire of Heraclitus is Logos, primordial consciousness, mostly unspoken (ἄρρητος). Politically, following Aristotle, the political is the distinctive property of logos: our capacity to judge just and unjust.
more: Logos in her teaching is not thinking. In the Pythagoras lesson it is first a ratio, a:b, the number behind every frequency, and then the energy of consciousness itself, the ancient νοῦς that perceives thoughts and emotions, observes and creates. It is one and common to all, the κοινὸς λόγος of Heraclitus, which the Greeks of 1940 joined when they left their borders behind.

In Heraclitus's sense the logos is the consciousness through which we perceive even our own personhood, and on waking we find it one and common. She insists that logos is not mind: it shows itself through the mind without being exhausted by it. As discursive reasoning, though, logos is multiple and plunges into number, so it must give way before the simple One.

label: Truth
take: Truth for her is simple and has no content: it is a state, not a set of propositions or rules ('not the Ten Commandments'), and propositions are true only by participation (μέθεξις) in it. She reads ἀλήθεια as non-forgetting or non-sleep, hears in 'αλ' a root of light as in ἥλιος, and tentatively sees an anagram of θήλεια, female, because truth keeps giving birth. Truth does not come to you; you come to the truth, which waits here already.
more: Truth is a state of consciousness, not an opinion, an angle or a list of propositions. Its first etymology is the removal of λήθη, forgetting, so truth is subtractive, like death: you strip away rather than add. It is often paradoxical, παρὰ τὴν δόξαν, because the cave is the realm of opinion and no opinion as such can be true. In the Sun simile truth is the immaterial light of the Good, which she distinguishes from mere reality.

Plato calls the light of the Good ἀλήθεια: it mediates between the One and our intellection, as sunlight mediates between sun and eye. The ancients spoke of 'touching truth' (ἐφάπτεσθαι τῆς ἀληθείας), and she hears in the verb both touching and being set alight.

label: Lethe, forgetting
take: Lethe, forgetting, is what the soul drinks on its descent: it falls from the ever-being into the illusion of the body-tomb-cave. The chains of the cave are λήθη, and the prisoners sleep in the cosmic dream. Asked what is opposite to Being, she says nothing is: within Being there is only the possibility of forgetting itself, and Lethe is the price God pays to manifest and play. Truth, which says 'change', is almost unbearable to someone still in λήθη.

In the 28 October talk she reads ἠλίθιος, the idiot, as someone who lives 'in lethe', having forgotten that he is one with his fellow citizens and with everything.

label: Second birth of the soul
take: The Orphic, Pythagorean, Eleusinian and Platonic traditions call the awakening of consciousness, while still in the body, a second birth, and she reads Christmas and the ancient Heliougenna as its festival. She maps it as a real pregnancy: a hidden conception below the radar of senses and mind, gestation nourished by love, teaching and virtue, labour pains with a midwife-teacher, a sudden birth into light, then nourishment and strengthening. The newborn is a revelation of what we always were, new and always ancient. Even knowledge follows this pattern: it must be conceived, carried and born in you.
more: The cave is womb and tomb, so leaving it is both a death and a second birth, a resurrection (ἀνάστασις). The soul that hears the call of return is gestated in the middle stage and reborn into the divine level, arriving 'suddenly'. Yet the second birth is not really a birth: you recognise that what you are was never born, never dies, and was never other than the infinite self of the All.

At the winter solstice nature strips itself, which is why Heracles, the Sun and, in the later appropriation, Christ are born then. In the soul this is the birth of the inner hero or sun after the descent: the three days the sun 'stands' mean the hero is sown, gestated and born, and 25 December is the birth of the sun. The new birth is your own truth shining, the birth of the χρηστός (useful) human who has found their true need and can benefit all beings.

label: The sudden
take: Ἐξαίφνης, Plato's 'suddenly', is her favourite Platonic word in the podcast: the moment the prisoner is released, or the soul is born into light when its hour is ripe. It does not depend on the human mind but on cosmic law (νομοτέλεια); other traditions call it providence, and it belongs to mystery, which holds the highest place in philosophy. It can come as loss, divorce, ruin or depression, or as an inspiration and the love of one's life, a 'good suddenly'. Either way it shakes a boxed, repetitive life awake.
more: Plato, she says, uses the 'much-longed-for' ἐξαίφνης three times in the cave: the breaking of the chains and every stage of awakening happen suddenly, and Plato does not explain how. Yet the sudden is preceded by long preparation, so awakening is both gradual and sudden. She identifies the ἐξαίφνης with the soul's ripe hour, also called grace.

Awakening arrives 'suddenly', the Platonic and Socratic ἐξαίφνης: it cannot be controlled or triggered like pressing a code, because its cause does not lie in the one trying. It is ἀμήχανον, not the product of time, method or knowledge, and is sometimes called divine grace or the Χάριτες. Yet, citing a teacher she calls 'the Indian Socrates', she adds that the suddenness is preceded by long preparation and ripening.

label: Transcendence
take: Transcendence is the first of the two movements of philosophy: closing the eyes (μύω), turning away from becoming and finding the One 'beyond'. She calls the belief that truth lies somewhere else a useful 'intermediate falsehood' that helps the soul turn inward. It corresponds to leaving the cave, deconstructing every conjecture, belief and even idea, up to the mystics' 'devouring fire'. But the soul cannot stay above, so transcendence is only half of initiation.
more: In the Neoplatonic formula she cites, enlightenment is transcendent, 'I leave the material', but this is only half: remaining only in the absolute is still dualism. The Good itself is 'beyond' (ἐπέκεινα) knowledge and being.

label: Immanence
take: Immanence is the second and longer movement: returning to the cave to recognise that the One remains in everything, here and now. She glosses ἐμμένεια as ἐν + μένω, the One that dwells everywhere, and illustrates it with Odysseus who, after reaching Ithaca, must still slay the suitors, that is, bring light to old habits and programming and integrate them. In daily life it means seeing the One at the tax office, on Taxisnet, in emails and morning coffee. The freed return out of love and justice and live on the razor's edge of the One and the many.
more: Leaving the cave is not the end: the circle closes only when the freed one descends into becoming, not only from compassion but because the apprenticeship is incomplete until then. The Neoplatonists called enlightenment transcendent and also ἐμμένεια, 'remaining in'. Back in the cave one sees that cave and Good are not two, that all is the Good, and that even illusion is awakening that forgets itself.

The Neoplatonists debated whether the One is in the world or beyond it, and Plato can be read both ways: the cave points to transcendent Ideas, while Diotima and the Phaedrus show beauty passing through everything. She holds that immanence characterises Hellenism more: God is everywhere and in everyone. This is why the Greeks engaged with polis and art, and why she links lingering transcendentalism to the abuse of nature.

label: Death and the practice of dying
take: From the One's perspective, birth into the body is a death and physical death is a return. The first definition of philosophy (Phaedo 64) is μελέτη θανάτου, practice of dying, but the death she means is the death of illusion and of the personality, dis-identifying from the body rather than leaving it. It is a daily process, removing one identification at a time, which is why Socrates says both 'dying' and 'being dead'. For those below the freed one has died, for those above he was born, and when he returns he seems risen from the dead.
more: For her there is no death, only sleep, dream and awakening. Life is the divine dream of Hestia, essence, and death ends the dream: a transition, a λύσις or untying of the cords between soul and body, which calls for courage and clarity and should be prepared for in peacetime. In the Platonic talks death is also what the philosopher rehearses while alive: the death of the illusory self, after which one 'simply goes on being'.

label: Soul
take: The soul is the vehicle of nous, formed when fiery nous 'cools'; she plays on ψυχή and ψύχω, to cool. It contains the body rather than the reverse: the Timaeus has the soul embracing the body, and what lies outside the body is our aura. In her reading the soul is ἀγαθοειδής, Good-like, carrying a little fiery sun, and in Plato the soul, not the body, is the true subject of politics. It descends by putting on tunics and ascends by taking them off until it is naked.
more: Following the Timaeus and Proclus, she teaches that the soul is not an object like an invisible bottle but self-moving motion, 'a verb, not a noun': two harmonised circular orbits, the Same and the Other, crossing in a χ. The body is inside the soul, not the soul inside the body, and the part of the soul beyond the body is what we now call the aura. Its essence (οὐσία) is never disturbed by what happens to it; only its revolutions are.

Soul is localised consciousness, energy cooled relative to the divine fire (she links ψυχή to ψύχω, to cool), and it in turn projects matter. Following Pythagoras she says we are divine souls having a dreamlike human experience. The soul has faculties to study (mind, heart, will and appetite; Plato's three parts), and the Odyssey is the archetypal map of its descent and return.

label: The One
take: The One is the ultimate nature of self and cosmos in the Orphic-Platonic-Pythagorean line she calls ancestral: ineffable (ἄρρητον), unknowable (ἄγνωστον), ungraspable (ἄληπτον) and unparticipated (ἀμέθεκτον). It is not a 'something' but an over-full nothing, a boundless radiance that is transcendent and immanent at once: all is in it and it is in all. It shines through every form like one light through the windows of many rooms, and it waits for us to see it rather than us waiting for it.
more: The One is the ineffable source, before even awareness, from which everything cascades and which is present in everything. Philosophy's goal has four names for one end (eudaimonia, gnosis, union and knowledge of the true self), and union is the close of a divine love affair in which two collapse into one. It is less a gain than a remembering, as in the Meno's recollection (ἀνάμνησις), and it requires shedding everything we are not.

The One is not a lifeless abstraction but living, rational, self-aware divine consciousness, the source from which all forms rise and to which they return. It is not far away: following Plotinus, it waits for us, and we only remove what covers it. All the talks rest on the Heraclitean principle that the One is in all and all is one, so a self that is separate, a 'private' interest or a bordered nation is a form of sleep.

label: Know thyself
take: She reads Apollo's Delphic command in two stages. First we take it to mean knowing our personality, preferences, body and the three parts of the soul, and that stage is valid. But at the level of being it asks us to know THE self, which is one in the universe: 'know that which knows', the observer who has thoughts, emotions and a body but is none of them. It is the foundational precept that turns the soul's eye inward, and a life not lit by it is, she says, harder than the effort of self-knowledge.
more: Apollo's own precept at Delphi, which she reads as the god's riddle in place of a welcome: if you want to know me, know yourself. Joined with the cryptic E ("you are"), it says you already are what you seek. It is her standard advice to anyone: turn attention from outside to inside and keep asking who you are, because the self is the one foundation that cannot be taken away.

She reads the Delphic maxim not as 'study your separate personality' but as Apollo calling consciousness to turn its eye on itself and know itself as pure knowing, the one Self. The command is singular ('thyself', not 'yourselves'), and she says the elided inscription could also read 'know it'. It marries ontology (σαυτόν: who am I) and epistemology (γνῶθι: how do I know), and whoever follows it finds that the one they thought they were does not exist.

label: The Sun
take: In her reading of Plato's Sun simile, which she calls 'Platonic trigonometry', the eye is the most sun-like organ and stores the sun's light; likewise the soul is Good-like and carries a small fiery sun within. The sun is self-luminous while objects are lit by another, and it causes growth without being any of them, as the Good causes knowledge. Its light is truth and its heat is eros. The goal is a stability beyond the solstices, the 'ever-living sun', from whose point of view there is no waxing or waning.
more: The sun is the visible symbol of the pure One and of spirit, so dismissing ancient 'sun worship' as primitive is, for her, an ignorant reading. In the Cave the sun is the Good, and the Sun above the Ideas is her image of the One beyond even the Ideas. After awakening there is no 'awakened person', only the Sun; and your inner sun was never in danger, since it never took part in the drama and only shines.

She walks through the Sun simile as the key to the Cave: eye, visible objects and sun form a triangle, and light is the 'third kind' that makes sight possible. The sun does not put sight into the eye but activates a power already there, which for her defines education. Its lord is Apollo, who takes us away from the many.

label: Light
take: Light is her constant image of spirit: the One is a boundless radiance (φωταύγεια, διαύγεια) that spreads like light through the windows of many rooms while staying one. The soul feeds on light, λόγος and realisations, and words are small vehicles carrying that light. She distinguishes three lights by their roots: sensible (ἡλ-, as in ἥλιος), spiritual (ἑλ-, as in Ἕλλην) and uncreated (the third root is uncertain).
more: Light is the mediating condition: in the visible field it lets the eye see, and in the intelligible field its name is truth. To think something is like lighting it so that it becomes intelligible. In the end she says there are not two, light and darkness: darkness is light very much dimmed.

Every light is an outflow (ἀπορροή) of fire and presupposes a fire, so in Corinth she moves 'from the gates of light to the source of light'. In the Sun simile light is the hidden fourth term, the 'third kind': without it we see nothing, yet we never see light itself, only objects. She derives φαίνεσθαι, to appear, from φῶς: whatever appears is light woven into forms through the Ideas, like the single light on a cinema screen.

label: Being and non-being
take: Following Parmenides, only what always is, is; for the ancients 'is not' means 'is not true', not 'does not exist'. Whatever rises and sets, sometimes is and sometimes is not, has the quality of non-being: bodies, thoughts, emotions, war and peace, economic booms and busts. Hence Parmenides' reversal: what seems to be is not, and what seems not to be (the invisible, intelligible) truly is. Being has no opposite; being and non-being are not two but one.
more: What she finds most innovative in the similes is that the five modes of knowing correspond to Plato's ontology, five functions or levels of being, so the Cave is a synthesis of epistemology and ontology. On the ontological side the shadows 'seem to exist but do not', being only an emanation or echo of formed objects.

She derives Ismenios from ἴσμεν, 'we know', which echoes ἐσμέν, 'we are': at the fourth step we know being. The archer's focus, ἑστία, is οὐσία. Seekers must not confuse the phenomenon with the essence.

label: Becoming
take: Becoming is the realm where nothing stays, so everything dies every moment: we live but do not live. She draws it under a 'T' on the board, below the world of rest, as Plato's world of otherness where the pairs of opposites live, and links it to water and Poseidon, the sea of emotions and beliefs. It is a mirror showing an inverted image, a 'drama of the mind' that sees dualistically. Pain within becoming is the alarm clock telling the soul to change.
more: Becoming is Heraclitus' river into which the soul's circles are plunged at birth, a 'first baptism' she also sees in Odysseus crossing Poseidon's waves. Nothing in this world of relativity can describe awakening, and paideia turns the soul from it toward Being. Yet becoming is not evil: it is the moving god called matter, the stage where divine qualities pass from potential to actual. The Titans, from τείνω, are its tensions pulling us off centre.

Plato adds a third category between Being and non-being: becoming, what 'is and is not', permanent now but soon a memory in the archives of the universal mind. Only what does not change meets the criterion of truth, so body, emotions, desires and thoughts all fail it. Becoming is also the middle stage of the path, the apprenticeship and pregnancy where the soul turns, and eudaimonia cannot be invested in it.

label: Philosophy
take: For her, philosophy is a lived spiritual path whose aim is the fulfilment of human nature: to be whole, free and happy. It starts as a love affair, an Eros for truth, and the mind serves only its first steps before it must let go into what contains it; wisdom is not acquired but activated, the clarity of our own being knowing itself. What universities teach today (arguments, polemics, the history of ideas) is in her view only the shell of what its founders defined as a path of awakening.
more: Philosophy for her is not a scholastic training in logic and argument, which is what it 'degenerated into', but a path to touch truth and a practice of death. Pythagoras coined the word as φιλότης toward wisdom, so it starts in the heart with the art of loving. Its aim is union with the Monad, and it moves in two beats: death and rebirth, or awakening and then embodying it as work in the world.

Philosophy in its ancient sense is eros for wisdom (φιλότης + σοφία), aiming at union with wisdom rather than mental knowledge, and Aristotle called it the science of sciences. It is a gift we give ourselves because every concept carries light to the soul, but it must become a path of steps toward eudaimonia and not a mental 'sport'. Philosophy is born where being and becoming cross: wholly lost in becoming we are mechanical, and in pure eternity there is nothing to say.

label: The political
take: For the Greeks politics is human nature, not a contract: we are by nature political animals, and the polis exists by nature, prior even to family and individual. So 'I'm not political' is itself a political stance, a frustration of that nature, and today's depoliticisation goes with a 'de-naturalisation'. Plato's polis mirrors the citizen's soul (her 'psycho-politics'), the lawgiver shapes character, and the true polity's shared purpose is awakening. Real participation means judging and ruling together in spaces of logos, not a four-yearly 'political ritual'.
more: Politics here is a stage of consciousness: after union, one returns to the many to harmonise them for the common good. Socrates was the true political man walking the agora, condemned by pseudo-politicians who loved money and power, and she asks from what vision anyone can govern who does not know who they are. The last step, Leschenorios, is a life shared in dialogue for the common good: 'not I but we'. The eros talk adds that even political relationships are erotic in nature.

Politics for her starts in the soul and returns to the world. The highest Pythagorean initiation was political, and eudaimonia is collective, the goal of the polity. She derives πολιτική from πόλος, pole, so every city is a field of forces that draws energies according to the inner state of its people. True politics is a «No» to vice and ego, attunement to the common logos, then a return to build foundations in which a civilisation blossoms.

label: Aristotle
take: Aristotle appears as Alexander's teacher, who gave him εὖ ζῆν, and as the source of her political anthropology: man is by nature a political animal, the polis exists by nature, and the citizen shares in judging and ruling. She uses his principle that science starts from 'what it is' (τί ἐστι), his view that εὖ ζῆν is the purpose of life and of politics, and his claim that the Good moves things 'as the beloved'. She says that for him γενναιότητα is the first moral virtue.
more: Aristotle supplies her with ἐντελέχεια and the olive seed, eudaimonia as the human entelechy, virtue that brings eudaimonia when sustained, the innate appetite (ὄρεξις) to learn, and 'the human being is a political animal' against the social contract. His On the Soul she calls the starting point of modern psychology. In the radio interview she adds that Newton's 'giants' were chiefly Aristotle, a claim she bases on his notebooks.

She uses Aristotle for the logic of ends: eudaimonia is the final cause behind every act, with nothing behind it, and it is our ἐντελέχεια. His seed of walnut or oak, carrying the whole tree and an impulse to grow even in poor soil, is her image of the soul tending to eudaimonia because it comes from it. He also supplies 'the human is a political animal' and calls philosophy the science of sciences; she notes he studied at Plato's school from 17 to 37.

label: Awakening
take: For her the fashionable word 'awakening' belongs to consciousness, not to the body (though it finally includes it) and not even to the soul, whose awakening is only one stage. Reality is already awake as living logos and self-knowing nous; only we sleep and wake, so nothing changes in the world and everything changes in us. It is not a spectacle of visions or miracles but an often unnoticed inner shift of vision, like veils lifting, and she maps it as five ordered steps named after Apollo. In the eros talk the erotic path is itself a path of awakening, which she equates with eudaimonia and freedom.
more: For her, awakening is not an experience, vision, energy event, emotion or insight, because every experience happens inside a limit while awakening concerns the infinite. It is the beholding (θέασις) of the One: a recognition without knowledge, a witness in which the separate 'you' disappears and you see you were always awake. It cannot be manufactured by time or method; it comes suddenly, usually after long ripening. The modern word stands for what the ancients called λύσις, liberation and εὐδαιμονία.

She defines awakening as an ineffable realisation, a beholding in which nothing changes: only the true nature of the self and of the whole as one is seen. Because the word implies a sleeper, she prefers the ancient θέασις, and she calls 'the awakened person' one of the greatest illusions, since such an identity keeps a gap between the ego and the pure 'I am'. It is not a political revelation, an energy experience or an out-of-body state.

label: Non-duality
take: She reads the Greek tradition as non-dual: in Plotinus' witness the seer and the seen are one, a union (ἕνωσις) other cultures call yoga. Diotima's negative description of absolute beauty is for her 'a wonderful non-dual description', the most language can do beyond the duality it is built for. She also rejects the dualist Plato in which sensible and intelligible are enemies; for her they are one continuum, and at the deepest level the inside and outside of the cave are one.
more: She teaches two ways to live, polarised and a-polarised, and coins the verb 'απολώσου': get un-polarised. Apollo takes no pole and no side, and removing the poles lets the One appear. Dual statements are both true and untrue (her 'right or left?' gesture), and the three approaches to a god are all true at once. In the eros talk: 'there is the individual and there is no individual', and in reality there are no others.

She argues that a large non-dual corpus lies hidden in the Presocratic, Socratic and Neoplatonic texts, above all Plotinus, ignored first by Christian theology and then by reductionist academia. Greek thought contains both a direct path and a graded education. Duality and non-duality are not opposed but dance together, and her ontology is a non-dual account of the dual world.

label: Winter solstice
take: The winter solstice, when the sun seems to stand still and then climbs again, is for her the soul's deepest dive into the body, the longest night and 'dark night of the soul' before rebirth. Christmas falls four days later because for the Pythagoreans four is establishment, the cube: what was performed in the depths is consolidated. She treats solstices and equinoxes as days of highest energetic inflow around which the ancient festival calendar was built. Yet from the sun's own point of view there is no waxing or waning at all.
more: She reads the four astronomical turnings as energy gates whose visible pattern mirrors movements of consciousness, on the Hermetic principle 'as below, so above'. Each turning (τροπή) releases food (τροφή) for the soul. At an equinox the soul's two circles meet, a moment of balance and sowing; at a solstice they are farthest apart, a crisis that can birth the inner hero. They are fertile conditions, not requirements: the best moment is always now.

label: Body
take: Life in the body is, from the One's view, the field of death: σῶμα σῆμα, the body as tomb, the Cave, the soul's winter solstice. Yet awakening happens without leaving the body, by dis-identifying from it. The body is the vehicle of the soul and is contained by it, not the reverse. Politically she criticises the modern individual understood as a body, the subject of science and biopolitics, set in the place of soul and consciousness.
more: She inverts the usual picture: the soul does not enter the body; the body enters the soul and is embraced by it. Plato calls the body a seat of continual inflow and outflow, porous, breathing, always exchanging with the great river of life. The body does not sense; it is a set of gates through which the river's motions reach the soul, which is why a body without soul senses nothing. The soul's overflow beyond the body is the aura.

Opinions, factions and ideologies rest on the belief that 'I am the body and others are bodies'. Racial origin refers only to the body, so dividing people by race identifies the human with the body, a materialist way of seeing.

label: Wisdom
take: Wisdom is living awareness (ἐπίγνωσις) in contact with the here and now, where life itself tells you what is what. Using the Cratylus she ties σοφία to light and to ὁρμή, motion, being connected with an ever-changing energy, and σύνεσις to 'going along with' things like an alert general. The dry soul is the wisest, warmed by the fire of the Good. Pythagoras, she says, knew that love (φιλότης) and wisdom go together.
more: Wisdom is linked with light, the light of understanding and realisation (her etymology, flagged uncertain). Philosophy seeks to merge with it, not to collect information about it. Her chosen line from Plato sets its moral condition: all knowledge severed from justice and the other virtues is cunning, not wisdom.

She draws her first practical proposal from the 'sophia' in philosophy: observe the mind, do not take what we believe for granted, and open a space between what I think and the I that watches it. 'There lies the key.'

label: Freedom
take: She asks us to celebrate freedom not as a memory but as the present state of our existence. Splitting ἐλευθερία, with an omega slipped under its omicron, she finds light (Ἑλ), the good (εὖ) and the eros that warms (θέρ-, ἔρως): freedom is eros, which is why a «Yes» must follow the «No». In the other talks freedom is what the free hands of the cave prisoners already hold and what self-inquiry finds at the root of awareness.
more: Freedom is inner before it is outer: Marcus Aurelius and Diogenes show one can be free even in prison, and every situation has an 'exit of freedom'. In her reading ἐλευθερία 'has ἔρως inside it': people make their greatest revolutions out of love, as the fighters of 1821 were drunk on love of freedom. Recognising one's true nature as fire and as the Good is freedom and leaving the cave. The reborn soul is free and joyful like a child, but a wise child.

Freedom is one of the universal aims philosophy fulfils, with wholeness and happiness. The Golden Verses say that if you leave the body for the free aether you become an immortal god: if, not when, so liberation is available now whenever we stop clinging to the body. Later Hellenic teachings, she says, describe an inner freedom and a happiness free from circumstances.

label: Free will
take: In her reading the prisoners of the cave are chained by legs and neck but not by the hands, and hands stand for free will, an extension of the heart, which can never be subjugated. So the first ingredient of liberation is wanting it: no mother, partner or child can change you from outside, except perhaps divine grace. 'Even the universe respects free will', so leave the door open a little. Wanting starts to turn the wheels of soul and life and draws events.

label: Respecting shame
take: She offers the Delphic maxim αἰσχύνην σέβου, 'respect shame', as a healthy alternative to self-flagellation, which she calls a pathological relation to conscience. Αἰδώς is the restraint felt before a wrong act, αἰσχύνη what one feels after it; respecting shame means respecting the self-regulation of justice within you. The ego hides from its Erinyes and from solitude; instead one sees the error, learns, adjusts and moves on. Feeling shame is healthy; feeling nothing is the danger.

label: Socrates
take: Socrates' 'I know one thing, that I know nothing' is the method that opens the pores of ἀπορία so Apollo can reveal himself. His daimonion told him only 'make music and work at it', meaning reach the last step of harmonising the many, and he walked the agora as a true political man until pseudo-politicians condemned him. In the eros talk he learns from Diotima, calls the path an erotic pedagogy, and teaches that health is inner peace and illness an inner civil war.
more: Not an anti-mystical rationalist but a mystic of the agora: an Eleusinian initiate who called Diotima his greatest teacher and meditated all night at Potidaea. His novelty was an anthropocentric turn, bringing spiritual realisation down into ethics, law and politics. His knowing that he knows nothing is the same letting go of mind that Plotinus describes, and he defined the philosopher as a lover of truth, warning that knowledge without justice is dangerous.

Socrates is the figure behind most of her readings: he defines παιδεία as the turning of the soul, calls death λύσις and philosophy a practice of death, speaks of the eyes of the soul, and works as a midwife, not a teacher. In her retelling he meets death like an Olympic athlete stepping out to perform what he trained for, and his daimonion's 'make music' becomes the Pythagorean programme. For him, she says, the way to truth is subtraction, not acquisition.

label: Parmenides
take: She calls him 'grandfather Parmenides', near whom Socrates sprouted. From him she takes that only what always is, is, and non-being never was, and the reversal: what seems to be is not, what seems not to be, is. His line 'to think and to be are the same' grounds her view that to be is to be conscious and that we are waves of fire and intellection.

label: Plotinus
take: 'Beloved Plotinus' supplies her key descriptions of awakening: the seer is one with the seen, so it is not even a vision; you do not become someone else, 'another' wrapped around you departs; and the One waits for us to see it. His light passing from room to room images the one essence in many forms, and his 'let us flee to the beloved fatherland' turns the Odyssey into the soul's homecoming. She pairs him with θέασις and θέωσις, and with the call to become σύμπας.
more: She carries the Enneads with her and reads 'there were not two... not a vision but a union' as the best description of beholding. Plotinus calls the One your true self, says whoever unites with the One was always the One, and points to silence. She thinks he is little studied because his clearly non-dual teaching cannot be understood without being lived.

Plotinus supplies her highest statements about the One and the Good: it is nowhere, yet there is nowhere it is not; it comes 'like one who never left'; and when you know the Good you recognise it as yourself (Ennead VI.9). She also takes from him that nous is fluid and unified, not a thing. She reads Kazantzakis' 'even the One does not exist' as reaching the highest vision Plotinus describes.

label: Proclus
take: She speaks of 'beloved and fully awakened Proclus'. From him she takes that the soul descends by synthesis, adding foreign tunics, and ascends by analysis, removing what does not belong to it until it is naked (quoting a Chaldean oracle). His procession and return (πρόοδος, ἐπιστροφή) frame her two movements of transcendence and immanence. She also cites his derivation of the Titans from τείνω and, uncertainly, of Dionysus as 'two minds'.
more: Proclus is her guide to the Timaeus: newborn souls cannot yet navigate embodiment, sense turbulence disturbs the soul's revolutions but never its essence, and the soul is two circles in a χ. He supplies the ideal of the 'naked soul' stripped of false identifications, and the reading of heroes' parentage as soul-astronomy ('Proclus scored, Greeks 1-0'). He stands in her lineage after Plotinus and Iamblichus.

Proclus gives her two key ideas in the Ares lesson: incarnation as a 'divine sleep' and 'divine dream', and, in his commentary on the Republic, the contrast between Athena's war by union and Ares' war by division. In the second-birth talk she groups him with Plato, Socrates and Plotinus as agreeing that νοῦς halts at the threshold of the true, beyond which one must leap.

label: Diotima
take: Socrates' teacher, a priestess from Arcadia in her account, and in the Symposium the only surviving text where we see a woman teaching. Diotima defines philosophy as a path of Eros and lays out a ladder of love that Potari counts as seven levels, rising from interpersonal to political and cosmic love. Her erotic pedagogy is for Potari the education every age needs, and she also cleansed the karmic residue of the plague in Athens.
more: Diotima was Socrates' woman teacher, and she taught him that the path of self-knowledge, philosophy, awakening and freedom is an erotic journey. From her comes the claim that the goal of eros coincides with the goal of human life. Athena stresses that the wisest man had a woman as his teacher.

Diotima of Mantinea, a priestess, was Socrates' teacher, which she says schools do not tell us. Her ladder of eros rises from bodily attraction to souls, political love, the sciences, the arts and finally divine eros, merging into the ocean of life, an erotic union with the One. She also teaches that humans are pregnant in soul even more than in body, gestating logos and virtue. Potari attributes to her a 'sea of truth', which she reads as a fiery sea where all is united.

label: Apollo
take: Apollo, god of light and clarity, is for her the god of awakening itself. She builds a whole talk on nine keys: the four etymologies of his name in Plato's Cratylus and the five cult names in Plutarch's On the E at Delphi, read as five ordered steps with the etymologies as the passages between them. Her favourite reading is ἀ + πολλῶν, 'not of the many': he takes no side and removes the poles, and when the many go the One appears. Every etymology of his name, she says, has a subtractive and an additive side.
more: Following Plutarch and Plotinus, she says the Pythagoreans' code name for the One was Apollo, read as ἀ- + πολλῶν, 'not of the many': the boundless radiance beyond polarities, the 'zero' where opposing forces cancel. The philosophers also called νῦν, 'now', a name of Apollo. At Delphi it is Apollo who asks consciousness to know itself, and he shares Delphi with Dionysus, as the Same shares the soul with the Other.

She reads Ἀπόλλων as ἀ- plus πολλῶν, 'not of the many': in his highest aspect he symbolises the One, the single pole of the universe, which is why he is always shown young (unity is youth). Lord of sun and fire, he calls us at Delphi to know ourselves, that is, to find the inner fire. Leto, fleeing Lethe, bears him on Delos, 'the manifest', after Artemis. At Delphi he shakes hands with Dionysus, an image of the god-man.

label: Dionysus
take: Dionysus' birth at the winter solstice (the Dionysia, Heliougenna) is the ancient form of the sacred infant's birth, and Heraclitus says Dionysus and Hades are the same. He holds the initiatory mirror: the visible world is an inverted reflection, and the Titans dismember him as daily pulls fragment our attention. As god of theatre he teaches that each of us plays a role but is not the role. She cites a reading of his name as 'two minds' (δύο νοῦς), the dyadic mind that must pass through the drama.
more: Theatre belongs to Dionysus, and life is the cosmic drama in which the One plays all the roles; awakening means playing on 'the stage of Dionysus' consciously and with cheer. In the Titans myth the tensions of becoming tear Dionysus apart until only the heart remains, which Athena (wisdom) saves for rebirth. He holds Delphi in winter while Apollo is away, and she maps him onto the Circle of the Other.

Following Plutarch, she says Apollo and Dionysus are one: two states of the universe. Dionysus is the dyadic mind, the one becoming many; Apollo is the universe's fulfilment, the moment it 'catches fire' to return into unity in a luminous, non-material fire. Nietzsche, she tells an audience member, 'began from good premises', but Plutarch already treats the two as one.

label: Ares
take: She rescues Ares from the hot-headed war god of popular tales. In his higher form he is the upward impulse of birth (Aries, spring, the shoot breaking the soil) and the power that divides in order to restore justice and good order (εὐταξία). Following Proclus she sets him beside Athena: Athena is war by union at the intelligible level, Ares war by division in the sublunar, emotional world, and wisdom always outranks force. Purified and raised on a base of purity, his red fire becomes vital force, boundaries, health, frank speech and the courage the awakened need in the cave, which is why she calls him the god of peace.
more: She rejects the one-dimensional image of Ares as an impulsive, aggressive war god. In her reading he is the god of Peace and of Εὐνομία, good order under law, an inner and outer cosmic force whose higher function guards the Light, the Divine, Balance and Love. In the Orphic Hymn his βία means life-force, vitality and strength (σθένος), not violence. A complete spiritual path must integrate him: we must be fighters on the path of virtue and self-knowledge, which is why Plato's philosophers must also be guardians.

label: Hestia
take: In the Orphic sequence Hestia, read as οὐσία, essence, falls asleep into multiplicity and dreams the incarnation, so life is the divine dream and death its end. She is also the nucleus of Olympus around which Ares forms the outer shell. In the Pythagoras lesson the ἑστία is the sacred fire at the centre of the heart: light it before you speak of sacred things, so that the light becomes words.
more: Hestia never leaves the centre of Olympus while the other gods come and go, so she is her image of the Circle of the Same, the still centre of the soul. When 'you' are no longer the centre of your world, the centre becomes Hestia: pure beholding, the One. Your core is a fiery focal point (ἑστία), and the mean (μεσότης) is the hearth of virtue and eudaimonia.

Hestia keeps the ever-burning flame at the centre of Olympus, and she derives the name from ἐσσία/οὐσία, essence: our essence is that primordial flame. We have 'got it wet', like Odysseus soaked by Poseidon's waves, but it is always within. Philosophers speak of kindling the inner Hestia, and recollection happens when Hestia is lit at the centre of the mind.

label: Aion, the playing child

label: Odyssey
take: The Odyssey is her map of the soul's journey home (νόστος), which she pairs with νόστιμος, 'tasty': nothing is tastier than eudaimonia. Odysseus leaves Circe, Calypso and even the advanced Phaeacians, because high understanding is a station, not the goal: 'as long as you see something, you haven't reached Ithaca'. Her twist is that Odysseus does not return to Ithaca; he wakes up in Ithaca, because he was always there.
more: Not just literature but an archetypal account of the soul: its descent into becoming, its sufferings and lessons, and its νόστος home. The Presocratics, Plato and the Neoplatonists read it theologically, as a code of the soul's path. She reads the hero's name two ways: from ὀδύσσομαι (suffering) and, esoterically, as the journey from the two to the Good to the One.

Each soul is an Odysseus travelling from the One into the many and back to Ithaca, and we need companions for the return. The voyage home runs from book Α to Ν; from Ν to Ω he must slay the suitors, meaning bring light to old habits, passions and programming and integrate them, the long immanent stage. Odysseus tied to the mast is the inner axis that holds while fortune's wheel turns, and Odysseus soaked by Poseidon is our inner flame made wet by the passions.

label: Delphi
take: 'We are the oracle of Delphi': the old, stagnant chthonic forces occupying the sacred space of our soul are the Python in the oracle. At the first step knowledge is still mediated, as when we go to a Pythia who is 'somewhere else'; mantic knowing means becoming the oracle ourselves. There was a lesche at Delphi, the meeting place of the fifth step, and the Delphic γνῶθι σαυτόν names the erotic path.
more: Delphi is where Apollo, lord of sun and fire, calls us to know ourselves, which for her means recognising the inner fire. She draws two maxims from it: γνῶθι σαυτόν, her billboard motto, and αἰσχύνην σέβου, 'respect shame', which she attributes to one of the Seven Sages. At Delphi Apollo and Dionysus shake hands, which she reads as the god-man: divine and human nature as one equation to solve.

Delphi is where Apollo inscribes 'know thyself', which she reads as consciousness turning to itself, and 'κόσμιος γίνου', which she reads as 'become cosmic', not 'be polite'. 'Know thyself' is one of about 147 Delphic maxims. Dionysus holds Delphi for the three winter months and Apollo returns at the spring equinox, an image of the two natures uniting.

label: The Mysteries
take: The Orphic, Eleusinian, Kabeiric and Platonic traditions encode the second birth. She derives initiation (μύησις) from μύω, closing eyes and lips to turn inward, and says from μύησις comes κύησις, pregnancy: initiation is conception, gestation, birth. The Kabeiric procession led to 'the Child', Persephone's story traces descent and return, and the Eleusinian climax fell, she says, at the autumn equinox. Mystery holds the highest place in philosophy.
more: Embedded in philosophy is mystagogy, the hieratic, but not in today's religious sense. It was cut away when the new religion sought a monopoly on the divine, and after Justinian it went underground into alchemists and orders. She calls for putting mystagogy back 'on the central table of the Pythagoreans', without fear, and says we are the first generation in seventeen centuries free to do so.

She derives μύησις and μυστήριον from μύω, to close the eyes or mouth: initiation is closing the eyes to phenomena, and a mystery is secret not because it is forbidden but because it cannot be said. The highest grade, ἐποπτεία, is recognising sensible and intelligible as one. No special robe or place is needed, since the world is already God's Telesterion and the senses are its doors.

label: Maieutics
take: Socrates' art is midwifery: he speaks only with those already pregnant in soul and helps what is held in potential pass into actuality. label: Pain as a wake-up call
take: Pain, loss and grief in becoming are the soul's alarm clock, signals that something must change. Depression can be 'the cry of the soul' to be freed from the prison it built, a 'spiritual surgery' for someone whose mask has stuck, and its long sleep can be a passage from the sleep of routine to waking; she reframes 'depressed' as 'deep rest'. She speaks of her own loss of a loved one, and adds that help may be needed so the person does not get lost there. One may also need to be 'sufficiently disappointed by becoming' for the flame of eros to catch.
more: Pain, she says, is allowed in the drama of the world because it is the perfect motive toward truth. The torment of constant change, things good one moment and bad the next, wears us out until we say 'enough', and the soul, which never moved, keeps sensing that 'something here doesn't add up'. In the Pythagorean principles suffering comes from identifying with the part, and pain finally makes us say 'I am something far greater'.

Psychic pain can be a perfect gate: as in training, it hurts and leads to no pain. Athena hears π in πόνος, the sound of pressing (πιέζω): pain presses and pushes, and when nothing else moves us, divine providence presses out of love, so that pain becomes a gate of liberation.

label: Cosmos
take: 'This cosmos, the same for all' in Heraclitus means the totality of creation, every ontological level, and she sees parallel universes already implied. It was made by no god or human: it is self-manifesting fire, beyond space and time. The cosmos is ἔλλογος, rational and conscious, governed by mathematical laws that also govern human becoming, which is why our consciousness is collective. Through justice, the subtlest fire, it is always in balance.
more: The Greek cosmos is teleological: nothing is random, and everything born tends toward its purpose. The sensible cosmos mirrors the noetic one ('as below, so above'), and the soul's two circles mirror the celestial equator and the ecliptic. So the Delphic 'κόσμιος γίνου' does not mean good manners but 'recognise your cosmic nature': become whole, Plotinus' σύμπας, the world in you and you in the world.

Κόσμος also means ornament: the world is beautiful, ordered by harmony and law. What makes the all (πᾶν) a σύμπαν is the σύν of love, the cohesive force. The cosmos is governed by moral and spiritual as well as material laws, which a wise lawgiver studies and transcribes into ethics.

label: Consciousness
take: She reads συνείδησις as σύν + εἰδέναι: being present with the knowing, the seeing and self-knowledge, so that we are συνειδότες, witnesses of truth. Consciousness works like a searchlight: wherever its beam turns, it receives that experience. The essence of the world is already consciousness of itself, Aristotle's νόησις νοήσεως, so awakening is our consciousness turning toward what already is. Its clarity, our 'tuning', decides how the god appears to us.
more: Consciousness is one and common, not shut in a box labelled with your name; whoever wakes up sees this, as Heraclitus says. It flows from the One as νοῦς and continues as soul and matter, so there is no gap between mind and matter. She holds that today's physics and cosmology are showing that matter springs from an ocean of consciousness, and she names love as another word for this shared unity.

She holds that consciousness is primary and one and is not produced by the brain; matter is a way consciousness arranges itself to appear. The cave is 'a function of my consciousness': what I take myself to be decides how my consciousness works and what world I live in. Yet she also says that what awakening realises goes beyond even consciousness in the ordinary sense, and beyond the mind.

label: Virtue
take: Following an etymology she takes from Plato's Cratylus, she reads ἀρετή as 'ever-flowing' (ἀεὶ ῥεῖν): virtue is the soul's energy flowing freely, without blockages. Observing and knowing the soul restores that flow, which is why self-knowledge is therapeutic; in Pythagorean terms the virtues are the right intervals of the soul's music. Ethics is regulating the soul toward ἀρετή, which, sustained over time, brings eudaimonia, and like Heracles at the crossroads we choose it, or vice, at every moment.
more: Virtue is what the soul gestates together with logos (Diotima) and what nourishes the embryo of awakening. In the Leto story Artemis, whom she reads as ἀρετή, is born first, before Apollo the manifest light: out of forgetting comes virtue, then truth. Virtue is the mean that answers the twin errors of nihilism and hedonism, and justice brings one back to it. On the path of virtue, she says, we must be fighters like Ares.

She sets out the ancient ladder of virtues as the method of philosophy: first the ethical or political virtues, then the cathartic, then the paradigmatic, culminating in the hieratic or theological virtues found in nearly all ancient philosophers. The Republic teaches how to unite the soul's parts in a fine mean, and justice is the virtue of virtues.

label: Christmas and the Nativity
take: She reads Christmas as the latest coding of the archetype of the sacred infant, behind which stand the Dionysia and the Heliougenna. She decodes the Nativity line by line: the cave is Plato's Cave, the manger is the solar-plexus seat of the irrational powers, the two animals are spleen and liver, Mary (Despoina) is the soul, Joseph the doubting mind, Herod's soldiers the forces threatening the newborn, and the flight into Egypt keeping it hidden. She ends wishing 'Christougenna, Iliougenna, Alithiougenna': birth of Christ, of the sun, of truth.
more: Early theologians appropriated Platonic and Aristotelian elements but could not let philosophy stand as an alternative path to the divine. Some theology put God outside the world and demonised body and desire, which she links to the abuse of nature; the daimon itself was turned into a demon. She stresses respect for all traditions while naming the loss, and notes academia grew out of church institutions.

She traces the distortion of philosophy to the post-Christian era and the Middle Ages: the new religion wanted a monopoly on access to the divine, so a path promising union with divinity through philosophy, logic and science had to be cut. Justinian's decree in the 6th century forbade teaching mathematics, the mysteries and theology, sending the knowledge underground.

label: Science and spirit
take: She respects science absolutely, but when the sciences are studied only materialistically, Platonic epistemology places them among convictions and dogmas; even science can harbour fanaticism, as the medical debates of the previous two years showed. With Kuhn she says communities resist paradigm change from emotional investment, not lack of evidence. The ancient aim is to reunite philosophy's science with its spirituality, 'because the source of science is God who ever geometrises'.
more: She derives ἐπιστήμη from ἐπί + ἵσταμαι, standing above and seeing the whole, so nothing that is not holistic is scientific in the ancient sense. In the Greek tradition science and spirituality were one, and she predicts that science, 'sweating but successfully', will within decades prove spirituality and bring a renaissance. The Galileo Commission call she wrote asks what the humanities would look like if consciousness, not matter, is primary.

For the Greeks, studying the cosmos meant knowing the mind, nature and body of God: science is the mind's approach to the divine, mysticism the heart's, philosophy the spirit's. Science cannot reach the One, and knowledge detached from justice becomes dangerous, as in environmental damage. She sees physics moving to a consciousness-first paradigm that many scientists resist, like Galileo's colleagues refusing the telescope.

label: The true Self
take: The personality (περσόνα) is the sum of changing parts, a role with its costume and name, and identifying with it is the death philosophy undoes. Life is a theatre: the actor (ἠθοποιός) 'makes an ethos' by how he plays, but is not the role, and the task is to recognise who plays all the roles. Justice as 'doing one's own' refers to the one fiery Self, and acting justly is a two-way road to discovering it. The Titans, our outward tendencies, lock us into a role for every stimulus.
more: Knowing yourself has three levels, laid out like a temple: the outer self (body, mind, personality, the story of the small self), the inner self (the soul and its faculties) and the secret self, oneself as the One. To reach the last you become a naked soul, in Proclus's phrase, taking off every role. Material things, even the body, can be taken away, she says, but the self cannot.

The true self is the primary essence, the pure One, prior to every predicate such as 'Greek'. Plotinus recognises it as 'the self I always was' and calls the One your true, mystical, or simply everyday self. The suffering self that seems to seek the light is itself a shadow: who seeks the light, the shadow or the light?

label: The Titans
take: The Titans are not bad guys out there but our inner tendencies: following Proclus she derives the name from τείνω, to stretch or tend. They are the pull of the irrational nature toward externalisation, material and egoic pursuits. Their dismembering of the child Dionysus is daily life fragmenting attention among work, family and taxes, each pull creating a role we lock into, and so the chains of the cave form.

label: The Stoics
take: From the Stoics she takes ἀταραξία, inner peace as the core of εὖ ζῆν, and ἐκπύρωσις, the periodic ignition of the universe in which the seminal reasons (σπερματικοὶ λόγοι) lie as seeds of all forms. Marcus Aurelius, 'very close to my heart this period', teaches ἀπάθεια: happiness not invested in externals, which she distinguishes from indifference, and he shows one can be free even in prison. An unnamed later Stoic gives her the idea that nothing happens to me without my free will.
more: She cites Marcus Aurelius, 'the enlightened emperor, the Stoic', who ruled an empire at war yet lived the pure One, which the Stoics call the ἡγεμονικόν. From his notes to himself she takes two lessons: do not be 'Caesarified', do not identify with your role; and all people are siblings, children of the same nous.

label: Pythagoras
take: Pythagoras is for her the great initiate who coined the word philosophy and defined its aim as union with the Monad, a 'Greek yoga' that joins the Dionysian, Orphic way of the heart with the Apollonian, Ionian way of mind and science. Arriving between a fading priesthood and a rising science, he reformed Greek tradition, and his highest initiation was political. Above all he is a potential of our own soul: she decodes his name until she can say 'you are Pythagoras'.
more: The coiner of "philosophy", born on Samos around 580 BCE, who fused Orphic spirituality with Presocratic science. In her telling his birth was prophesied at Delphi, he studied for decades in Egypt and Persia, and Iamblichus saw him as an emanation of Apollo. His goal was union with the Monad and his method rests on four pillars; yet he came back to life, married a student, had children who led his school, and trained politicians.

The Pythagoreans described the fulfilment of existence as union with the Monad and gave the One the code name Apollo, 'not of the many'. They purified the senses through long silence and living apart, and saw truth as a sphere without circumference. label: Harmony
take: Harmony is not the absence of opposites but their sacred union: ἁρμός, a joint, together with κρᾶσις and μῖξις, blending and mixing. With the Pythagoreans she says that without opposition there is no harmony, so we should not fear conflict. Apollo's fourth power, ὁμοπολῶν, moves the poles together into a new unity. In the eros talk, eros is the weft of universal harmony that holds the world in one.
more: Justice is harmony of all levels, and φ is 'the rhythm of harmony': each level relates to every higher one through the same ratio, order and geometry. Establishing justice and harmony in the soul lets it be reflected outside, as above so below.

She derives ἁρμονία from ἁρμοί, joints, and ἀραρίσκω, to fit together: the healthy co-existence of everything in the universal polity, like the physicists' unified field where every vibration stands in proportion with all others. Health and harmony spread 'from end to end' of a social whole like organs in a body. Justice is the self-regulating fire that keeps the cosmos in this balance, and in his higher function Ares guards it.

label: Ethos and character
take: Ethics does not mean morality: from ἦθος and ἔθος, habit, it is the habitual way the energy of the soul moves, habits of consciousness. Plato's Academy taught it as moulding oneself into a balanced person, and she notes that ἠθική is an anagram of Ἰθάκη, so knowing the structure of the soul is the way home. Its fullest form is the ethics of love, summed up in the teaching that there are no others.
more: Character (ἦθος) comes from habituation (ἔθος), so the lawgiver is not a bureaucrat but a 'character-shaper' (ἠθοπλάστης) whose laws initiate the soul into values; this is why, for her, responsibility lies first with the polity. In the theatre of life the actor, ἠθοποιός, 'makes an ethos' by the way he plays his role. She adds that ἦθος also means τρόπος, which is also the word for a musical mode.

label: Courageous nobility
take: Courage is a hinge in two talks. In the Ares lesson the awakened need the courage of the spirited part, a virtue of both warrior and philosopher, or the cave will 'eat' them, and the soul needs fearlessness to cross the passage after death. In the 28 October talk the collective «No» of 1940 was possible only because Greeks had cultivated ἀνδρεία in their souls and were brave in daily life, so their bravery could show on the political level.

Without paideia to keep the soul in it, collective trauma breeds the 'trauma of resignation' she sees in modern Greeks. The Ares archetype makes the same point spiritually: we must be fighters on the path of virtue, and facing one's conscience means 'you must enter the war'.

Athena reads ἀνδρεία as ἀντί + ῥέω, going against the current: Socrates says the currents of injustice and illusion in the world are many, and like Theseus, Odysseus or Heracles one must find the strength (σθένος) to swim against them.

label: Persephone
take: In her Eleusinian reading Persephone's three names trace three stages of the soul. As 'bearer of death' (φέρουσα φόνον) she descends and lives the death of truth, identification with the body. As Φερσέφασσα, bearer of light, she carries the light that sets her on the path of gestation and stripping. As Φερέπαφα, bearer of touch, she touches the immortal and returns to Mother Demeter.

label: The senses
take: Against the idea that the spiritual must renounce the senses, she teaches that the philosopher purifies them. Sensation (Timaeus 43a-c) is the moment the river's waves, striking the body, reach the soul's circles; the sense organs are only gates, and it was never the body that sensed but the mind. Rightly understood, the senses are sacred gifts for enjoying God and one of the great initiations of embodied life: we reach fullness not through them but with them as allies.
more: Whoever trusts only what the five senses give still lives in the cave, she says, and seeking the exit through the senses only drives you deeper. Modern education cultivated the five senses and neglected the 'dozens' of the soul's senses, such as intuition, awareness and psychic sight, each a counterpart of a physical sense. As the saying goes, mind sees and mind hears: the soul can withdraw from the organs to turn toward itself.

Sight is the 'most sun-like' of the senses, since we see through light, and Plato uses it to lead us from the visible to the intelligible. Opinions about the sensible world sit inside the cave, and liberation includes freedom from the narrow frame in which we interpret the senses.

label: Smell and aroma
take: Smell has a special place: it lies between water and air, between sensible and intelligible, and goes straight to memory, so she calls it a direct gate to φρόνησις (which is 'not by chance' akin to ὄσφρησις, smell). Its double nature means a scent can lift the soul (pure flowers, incense, herbs) or drag it down (chemical blends and animal-based perfumes). Incense, θυμίαμα, 'reminds' us (her wordplay) and awakens the soul's Mnemosyne, and whatever we wear and exhale feeds a corresponding order of beings.

label: Love
take: Where eros is the drive toward union, ἀγάπη is the fullness of recognising it. Love is another name for the one, common unity of consciousness, so knowing yourself as love is the single cure for every ill, and love is the beginning of wisdom. Its ethics is concrete: love in word, thought, feeling and act, treating everything as your own household (οἶκος) and doing it selflessly, as Marcus Aurelius taught.
more: The first real mark of awakening is love in its range, fervour and universality: if nothing is separate and all is you, you cannot help loving everything, like a mother, whatever your sex or whether you are a parent. This love is impersonal and holds even where you disagree. In her own life the realisation of oneness brought an equanimity together with equal care for every form of life, with ethical consequences: others' well-being matters as much as your own.

What the ancients called cosmic eros we would today call the power of love: the glue holding the universe together. Every relationship, even the political, is erotic by nature. At the end of the path the divine daimon we are is held 'in the embrace of universal love'.

take: The winter solstice, the darkest night, is a privileged gate, not a misfortune: darkness means introversion, the time to descend like Persephone into the subconscious with the hero's torch. There you face your monsters, hidden passions and their roots in events, family and ancestors, uproot them and sow virtues.
