label: Hellenism
take: Hellenism for her is a universal spirit, not ethnocentric pride, built on two principles: Heraclitus' 'all is one' and 'as above, so below, as within, so without'. Its path was never lost: the golden chain lives in the soul's memory and is allowed again after centuries of bans. In the Pythagoras lesson she tells how a teacher in the Himalayas sent her home: the whole tradition of awakening was already in her own culture.
more: Hellenism is not the era after Alexander but a living worldview and spiritual path, and she prefers "Hellenic" to "Greek". It leans to immanence while holding transcendence, and it offers a secular spirituality without the devotional side of Eastern paths. It is a treasure Greeks are sitting on: a Westerner seeking spirit need not run East, since it is already in this root.

Hellenism's distinctive gift, for her, is that science and spirituality are one path: science itself is the way of awakening. She calls the Republic 'the Bible of Hellenism' and traces a lineage from Orpheus (thousands of years ago) through Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle to Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus and Damascius. She links Ἕλλην to the root of spiritual light and calls the holistic Greek worldview a treasury we must return to.

label: Myth as symbol
take: Myths are theology in the psyche's native symbolic language: mythology is initiation (μύηση) into theology. Homer coded cosmic and karmic laws in analogies, such as Apollo's anger standing for the reaction our actions bring back. Children read such stories literally, which is why Plato filtered tales of jealous or warring gods.

Ancient texts are likewise gates, not texts: since truth is infinite, the interpretation of an allegory can never be finished.

take: Behind every desire that seeks expression through the senses, the soul is seeking the fullness (κόρος) of the Good, so desire is sacred in its motive. Only wrong education makes it believe fullness lies in one more possession or meal, which breeds the ἀκόρεστον, the insatiable, and explains why many wealthy people are unhappy. label: The separate self
take: Any identity, even 'the awakened one', sets itself against something else and so keeps a gap between the ego and the pure 'I am', between the ego and the One. She lists the false identities in order: I am my role, then my convictions (left, right, Greek, Platonist), then my knowledge (philosopher, scientist, knower), 'again a trap'. Threatened identity is why scholars and scientific communities resist what they do not understand.
more: What falls away in awakening is the belief that you are a separate person, body, soul or mind: in Plotinus' terms not becoming someone else, but 'another' that had wrapped itself around you departing. The separate self is a story, 'a shadow from the cave'. Hence 'an awakened person' is a contradiction, and ego-centred goals (proving yourself, possessions, fame) lose their pull: whom would you be serving?

Athena pictures the stream of thoughts as a labyrinth circling the Minotaur, the ego, to whose centre one must go like Theseus. From the start, Athena says, philosophy was a path of love whose aim was to free us from the ego.

label: Daimon
take: Not the Christian demon but the inner true self, a droplet of God and the inner teacher. She derives it from δαίω, I burn, tying it to Heraclitus's ever-living fire, and from a sense of distributing: each daimon is a localised share of the one fire. Eudaimonia is then that flame touching its own good nature.
more: She derives δαίμων from δαήμων, 'one who knows and teaches', and from δαίω, 'I am aflame' (her readings): the daimon is a fiery self-awareness that teaches and reveals because it knows. No one from outside makes you eudaimon; at your core you are this flame of truth. Eudaimonia is known only as daimones and pure minds, never as roles, costumes or personalities.

The δαίμων is the inner flame, voice and compass, a spark that never slept, 'the one who knows'. She derives it both from knowing and from δαίω, to burn (cf. δάδα, torch), so touching truth rekindles it. Socrates' daimonion is his inner teacher, the voice of Apollonian consciousness, and εὐδαιμονία is this daimon freed to express the divinity at its core.

label: Zeus
take: Zeus is consciousness in its creative operation, the cosmic mind. His endless loves and children are not literal: goddesses and mortal women are the divine and ordinary ideas that mind mingles with, and every birth is a world. She reads his two names as two movements, Δίας dividing and projecting, Ζεύς unifying and returning (etymologies she offers as her own).
more: In her reading Zeus is not someone out there but our νοῦς, our awareness: the goat Amalthea nursing infant Zeus is the soul-food released at the Capricorn solstice so that the nous remembers itself. Purified senses can perceive 'the vibration of Zeus', and she reads διάθεσις as 'Διὸς θέσις', the position of Zeus or spirit. She cites the Orphic Hymn to Zeus for a 'liberating witness' that is also a prayer.

There is no Apollo without Zeus, the demiurgic nous (after Proclus) that keeps generating ideas and natures, hence his many children. Apollo comes through creation to remind us not to get lost in phenomena but to return to the essence Zeus generates. Talk of Zeus being 'born' is a convention for the human mind: these are simultaneous, qualitative differentiations, not historical events.

label: Eastern parallels
take: She trained in India and found that meditation there cleared her lens until she could read Plato with new eyes: everything was already in her own tradition. She parallels Greek ideas with the Tao, Atman, Buddha nature and yoga, holding that truth is one. Yet the postwar West's turn East met cultural friction, and a message in the Himalayas told her that what she sought was where she started.
more: Having studied Hinduism, Buddhism and Taoism alongside the Greek tradition, she finds the same core under a different 'colour' given by culture, history and place. Those who realise awakening in any tradition live the same state. She draws on the Buddhist luminous void and calls philosophy, anachronistically, 'the yoga of the Greeks'.

She draws parallels with India and Tibet: Plotinus' ἕνωσις is what others call yoga, the Greek teacher dedicated to all beings mirrors the bodhisattva, and the Buddha's 'the right moment is now' matches the Greek νῦν. She links the divisions of the Circle of the Other to the seven chakras, and Autobiography of a Yogi turned her own life toward meditation in 2008.

label: Beholding (theasis)
take: θέασις, beholding, is how she says the Greek tradition names awakening: 'the beholding of the One', in which often nothing happens, no gate opens, no angel appears; you simply witness what already is. It shares a root with θέατρον and θεατής: we come into the divine theatre as spectators of truth. Her formula from the Republic is that a change of θέασις (seeing) leads to θέωσις (deification).
more: She says the ancient word for awakening is θέασις, beholding, not something that happens to you. Θέα and θέωσις contain θεός and θεά: to behold is to see what is already here waiting for you, what you are. Truth does not come to you; you come to it, and what shifts is the vision (μετατόπιση θέας), not the world.

For her θέασις is the ancient name for what we now call awakening: reaching the beholding of the Good, or touching truth. It is called beholding precisely because nothing is created and nothing happens; only a pure seeing arises. With Plotinus she says this seeing turns out to be union: there were not two.

label: The apophatic way
take: Because what is realised is ἄρρητον, belonging neither to words nor concepts, she begins by saying what awakening is not: apophatic theology or knowledge. Diotima does the same with absolute beauty (no body, no limbs, no colour). Her practical test follows: while you still see or understand 'something', even God or the light, do not stop; you have not reached Ithaca.
more: She defines awakening largely by what it is not: not a political revelation, not an out-of-body or energy experience, not small tastes. The Good is beyond knowledge and truth, ineffable, so whoever insists on knowing it is stuck at an earlier stage: one must let knowledge go to dive into the source.

label: Recollection (anamnesis)
take: All knowledge is recollection because the soul's essence is the essence of the cosmos and the divine: knowing is not shopping for something new but activating an imprint already within. Feeling a lack proves it, as you cannot look for keys you do not know you lost. Activating the soul's memory (μνημοσύνη) is, for the ancients, activating eudaimonia; incense 'reminds' us, and her own first reading of Plato at 14 felt like remembering.
more: With Plato she holds that all knowledge is recollection. Like an olive seed carrying the tree's genetic material, we carry 'psychic genetic material': the seeds of eudaimonia, knowledge and freedom, forgotten but never lost. In the Pythagoras lesson the path itself is stored in the soul's μνημοσύνη in the heart, and the name of Pythagoras' father, Mnesarchus, means memory ruling.

Plato says knowledge is recollection, so teaching means reminding: activating the innate power of ἰδεῖν rather than inserting knowledge. Following Plotinus, she adds that whoever comes into union with the One was always the One and simply remembered it.

label: The Circles of the Same and the Other
take: From the Timaeus and Proclus she teaches that the soul is two circular strips joined in a χ. The Circle of the Same, matching the celestial equator, is the Hestia within that keeps us centred in being; the Circle of the Other, matching the ecliptic and zodiac and divided into seven (she links these to the chakras and planets), carries senses, passions and changing moods. θάτερον is an anagram of θέατρον, the theatre of roles. True human life is their conscious union; equinox and solstice mark their meeting and their greatest distance.

label: Matter
take: Matter does not exist apart from consciousness: in the Platonic tradition it is an emanation (ἀπορροή), the last stage of the One's outflowing light, and 'the universe is noetic'. She calls matter-as-primary 'the biggest fake news', an interpretation of consciousness seen at a tilt. Still, the material world is no prison: a provident Demiurge made it as a sacred play of consciousness, and physicists' 'energy soup' is better called an 'energy river'.

label: Eternity and time

label: Telos and entelechy
take: The Greek universe is teleological: nothing is random, and everything tends dynamically toward its purpose, a force that constantly pulls us. Perfection (τελειότητα) is not an abstract ideal but the fulfilment of one's τέλος. Like a seed carrying the whole oak, the soul tends toward eudaimonia because it comes from eudaimonia: our origin is our Ithaca.

label: Aporia (not-knowing)
take: If I do not recognise that I do not know, I do not ask. Admitting not-knowing, Socrates' method, opens the pores (ἀπορία), and then Apollo starts to reveal himself. label: Purification
take: Purification runs through her teaching: cathartic virtues (diet, mantras, energy work, cleansing the luminous body that the Chaldean Oracles call the soul's subtle vehicle), Epimenides lifting karma from cities, Diotima cleansing the plague's residue, and tragedy purging audiences through imitation of heroes' passions. Such energetic cleansing, she stresses, is not only an Eastern or New Age idea but is in the Hellenic sources.
more: The philosopher's task in the Republic is to purify the senses, not renounce them: purified senses perceive 'the vibration of Zeus' and attune us to the One. Eudaimonia is a process of stripping (ἀπογύμνωσις) false beliefs, passions and self-images until one is a 'naked soul'. Pure aromas, flowers and incense cleanse and raise the aura, and simply facing your shadows with the wish for transformation begins the alchemy.

Apollo's first etymology, ἀπολούων, means washing: cleansing what we thought we knew, the views, poles and habits (ἕξεις) that cause suffering and war. Awakening is the lifting of veils as we clean, until clarity appears. Apollo also 'destroys' (ἀπόλλυμι), but only the useless, a good loss; and the Python's stagnant waters must flow for the soul's oracle to be cleansed.

label: Life as divine play
take: She calls the phenomenal world a δρώμενον, a sacred enactment, staged within the mind of God, who imagines or dreams it; in this sense it is a phantasm, at once collective and individual. Following Proclus, essence falls into a 'divine sleep' and dreams the many, and death ends the dream. These are her metaphysical views. Practically, the awakened watch the shadow play (she compares it to Karagiozis) while remembering 'I am not this'.
more: The second mark of awakening is εὐθυμία, a childlike cheer that comes from seeing life as Dionysus' divine theatre, where the One plays every role and we are spectators of truth. Heraclitus' Aeon is a child playing dice, the dice being the One's possibilities. You may still have to play a role, even a strict or serious one, but you play it without becoming it.

label: Athena (the goddess)
take: In the Ares lesson Athena is war 'by union': through providence and strategy she removes the monstrous and passionate so that beings reunite, using every other means before bloody war, and she always overpowers Ares because wisdom rules force. In the radio interview she names wisdom as the goddess's first virtue, joined by justice, temperance and discernment. Her birth from Zeus's head means wisdom is the fruiting (κάρπισμα) of mind, its τέλος.

label: Philotes, cosmic love
take: The Presocratic, above all Empedoclean, name for the cohesive, attractive force that makes the many into one universe; Empedocles said everything is ruled by attraction and repulsion, as physics now says too. To know ourselves as cosmic φιλότης is, for her, the panacea for separateness. Self-knowledge leads to it, and from it comes the Neoplatonic call to love all things.
more: Pythagoras defined philosophy as φιλότης toward wisdom, so the path begins by cultivating the art of loving, the purified heart. In the Ares lesson the Presocratics' two cosmic forces are Νεῖκος, strife or division, and Φιλότης, love or union: both are divine workers in the architecture of the cosmos, embodied by Ares and Athena.

The word philo-sophia says what must be activated first: φιλότης, love, cultivated together with consciousness until one remembers the One. Her second closing practice is φιλότης: training in love and kindness towards oneself and all beings. Love for all beings and for the common good is, for Plato, the precondition of politics.

label: The idiotes
take: In ancient Greece whoever cut himself off from the whole ('what do I care what society does') was an ἰδιώτης, and English kept the word as 'idiot'. She reads ἠλίθιος not as an insult but as a cognitive state: one who lives 'in lethe', having forgotten he is one with his fellow citizens and with everything. He sees himself as a little seashell in the ocean of the absolute, and she calls this a personal and collective disease of Greek society.
more: In ancient Greece the private person concerned only with his own interest was a negative figure who loses his human worth, his life spinning around ego and private affairs like an angular momentum (στροφορμή). English borrowed the word as "idiot" for good reason: failing to see that you are first a collective being is a kind of damage. Loving another person is the first step out of this state.

She contrasts the ἰδιώτης, the private person living 'for my own sake', with the πολίτης and κοσμοπολίτης of the last steps. Instead of waking up asking what to do for one's own little circle, one acts for the whole. She asks how much we do each day only to maintain an imaginary persona.

label: Symbol and archetype
take: A symbol carries something sensible (a king sailing to Troy and back) up to the intelligible level of the laws of human and cosmic nature. Jung's archetype is, in her view, a renaming of this Greek idea. Tragedy proves the point, since only living archetypes could produce catharsis; and for Greeks the Odyssey is a symbol, while Hollywood treats it as merchandise.
more: Awakening, like number, cannot be pointed at: 'two' appears in endless sensible forms yet is one idea, and the noetic cannot be reduced to the sensible. label: Ithaca and nostos
take: Νόστος, Odysseus' sweet homecoming, is what gives life its νοστιμιά, its flavour, and its eudaimonia. Yet arrival is not completion: Odysseus reaches Ithaca only mid-Odyssey and must still face the suitors, which she tentatively reads as our illusions, just as the freed prisoner returns to the cave. In the 28 October talk Ἰθάκη is an anagram of ἠθική: the passions toss us on stormy seas and make us lose our Ithaca, so coming home is ethics. With Cavafy, we meet the monsters on the way only if we carry them in our soul.

The goddess leads Odysseus not to a new continent but back to where he began, now changed and occupied by suitors. Her wordplay that ἠθική is an anagram of Ἰθάκη makes ethics the road home, and she stresses that return means renewal, not nostalgia.

Odysseus leaves Ithaca for the war of the many and must return; we too have fought long for the νόστιμον ἦμαρ, the day of return, which is eudaimonia, our home. She matches the journey to the Neoplatonic procession, remaining and return.

label: Plato's Republic
take: She calls it Plato's magnum opus: if all his other works were lost, its quintessence would survive in it. Subtitled 'On the Just', it begins in Piraeus with the question of justice and covers soul, virtues, constitutions, music, education, epistemology and life after death. It must be read whole, not in excerpts, and its core thesis is that the just city cannot exist outside unless it is first built in the soul.
more: She teaches the Republic almost every year, calls it the Bible of philosophy and an ark of knowledge, and wrote her LSE dissertation on it as an initiation. It presents a vision of realising the One through social and political structures, and its treatment of music and Homer is regulation, not banishment. Her course Building the Republic within and without reads the healthy city as a model for a healthy character, from which outer change follows.

label: The golden thread and its cut
take: She traces one lineage from Orpheus (an avatar and son of the Muses who founded the mysteries) through the Presocratics, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, the Stoics and the Neoplatonists, ended when Justinian closed the schools in 529 AD on pain of death. The spirit went underground and, she says, is now being rekindled in Greece as an indigenous path.

label: Spirituality and religion
take: She warns that spiritual people have been trained to be 'lukewarm water', soft and guilty about strength, and calls this a cave strategy to disarm awakening. Strong traditions (Greek, Hindu, Tibetan, Native American) pair the illuminated one with the warrior, and only declining traditions undermine the warrior. The more refined we are inside, the firmer we must be outside, and spiritual work is incomplete until it becomes action and life.
more: She hesitates over the word because of its religious ring: what Hellenism offers is a secular path into spirit without devotional aspects. Religion is organised spirituality that often loses its spirit and becomes politicised, as the Tao Te Ching says when the Tao is lost religion appears. Theological in the Greek sense does not mean religious, and calling philosophy mystical is unnecessary because that was its original meaning.

The Age of Aquarius brings both more searching for truth and unfiltered ideas: awakening as visions, beings from other stars, a body emitting light, walking on water. She calls this confusing the phenomenon with the essence. Signs and synchronicities belong to the second step, but the task is to stabilise them into a way of life, not to chase them.

label: The divine and the gods
take: There are three ways to approach any god, text or idea, all true at once: external, at the πρόναος ('I am here, Apollo is there'); internal, Orphic, where the god becomes a power of my soul; and central, mysteriac, where the god is lived as an active mode of being of the One. label: The Greek language
take: Greek is a performative, vibratory language: like Beethoven or a mantra it cannot truly be translated, and reading it in the original acts on soul and energy. label: Music and the Muses
take: Music is Apollo's fourth power and, for her, the art of harmonising opposites rather than playing an instrument. Socrates' daimonion told him 'make music and work at it', which she reads as reaching the last Apollonian step: having gone beyond the poles, return to the many and harmonise them. Like the freed prisoner going back into the cave, the philosopher must make music with others, which she calls the political step of consciousness. The aim is a stable, virtuous, 'musical' life.
more: She reads the command Socrates received in the Phaedo, 'make music', as the whole Pythagorean programme. Every psychic power is a frequency, every frequency a ratio of two numbers, so the soul is numbers dancing, and to make music is to tune the soul's inner arrangement by the laws of good order and rhythm, which in human terms are the virtues. That harmony becomes a gate to the One, and the words 'and work' send the realised one back to embody it in the world.

Music, meaning all the arts of the Muses, is to the soul what exercise is to the body, and political change begins with the musical modes a society listens to. Because ἦθος is crystallised vibration, Plato placed music under the lawgiver's care rather than banishing the poets. Listening is, she says, the most important spiritual act, and the Muses are doorways to essence.

label: Psycho-politics
take: Political regimes, she argues, match the psychic state of the people. When the desiring part (ἐπιθυμητικόν), fed by consumerism and advertising, seizes the reins from the heart's beat for freedom and the capacity for knowledge, a people gets an 'oligarchic tyranny' that calls itself democracy. So the first polity to govern is one's own soul: without self-mastery, from what position would you govern others?
more: From Plato she takes the idea that the soul comes first and generates constitutions. Hence her term psycho-political trauma: modern Greece, lacking smooth historical continuity and a settled identity, carries an unhealed wound, so when Hollywood treats a sacred symbol as merchandise (her cultural colonialism) the reaction is psychic, not racist. Healing the soul precedes political change.

People once said that to diagnose a polity you should look at its arts; she proposes looking at how its citizens approach eros: from which energy centre, with what vision, from what consciousness. As we approach eros, so we approach our collective union, which is also erotic. She suggests research into which kinds of eros different regimes and societies promote.

label: Crisis
take: Eras of crisis, she says, have always been more fertile for conceiving the seed of change: transformations follow a crisis. In the radio interview she reads the pandemic, harsh as it was, as a 'blessing' that forced the turning inward on everyone at once, as if life itself made us practise asceticism together and ask where the basis of our well-being lies. These are her interpretations of the crisis, offered as a spiritual reading. In the 28 October talk she warns that a force for change with no rooted values is soon swallowed by the old system.

label: The feminine in philosophy
take: Her Harvard research reclaims the feminine in two ways: historically, recovering forgotten women who shaped philosophy beyond Hypatia and Diotima, and epistemologically. Academia formed its methods when women were excluded, so its norms stay masculine and sideline emotion and psychology in knowing. The deeper call is a holistic education of mind, heart and ἦθος.

label: Fence of Olympus
take: Her favourite line of the hymn calls Ares the ἕρκος Ὀλύμπου, the fence or fortress of Olympus. She pictures him as the line of shields around the gods and as the outer electron shell around Hestia's nucleus: the outermost layer is the most exposed, which is why the myths show him straying and switching sides. Spiritually it means our centre is wisdom but our edges must be red, because creation, the soul and awakening all need guarded boundaries; she also links ὅρκος, the oath, to setting a boundary.

label: Practice of death
take: Her second definition of philosophy comes from the Phaedo: the philosopher accomplishes in life what fate accomplishes for everyone at death, the release of the soul from the body. She stresses that this means dis-identifying from the body, not leaving it, and that touching truth and dying are the same thing. She often quotes a modern teacher: if you die before you die, you will not die when you die.

label: Orpheus
take: In the Ares lesson Orpheus is the author of the hymn cycle, and the order of its last five hymns is itself a teaching. In the Pythagoras lesson she reads ΟΡΦΕΑΣ as an anagram of ΦΟΡΕΑΣ, the carrier of the flowing light, a first 'avatar' bearing Athena's primordial wisdom. The Orphic current is the heart-centred, ecstatic, Dionysian way that had degenerated by Pythagoras' time and that he reformed, and the Orphic teachers place the soul's memory in the ἦτορ, the spiritual heart.
more: The Orphics teach the internal approach to the gods: still dual, but the god becomes a power of my soul, and the task is to become Apollonian.

label: Know the knower
take: Her deepest reading of self-knowledge is to turn consciousness back on itself and ask who the one who knows is. You find no someone and no something, only boundlessness (ἀπεραντοσύνη), freedom, timelessness, calm and peace. This consciousness is the stable basis of every experience, pure knowing that knows itself and that, through its modifications, made the appearance of the many. She calls it easy, a meditation one can do now and repeat.

label: Dis-identification
take: Her own word for the Platonic separation of soul from body is αποταύτιση, dis-identification: not leaving the body but ceasing to take it for oneself. You have a body, emotions, desires and thoughts that change from age five to a hundred, while the 'I am' stays. Its fruit is freedom from the illusion of a self bounded by the skin, and in the radio interview it appears as undressing the roles and labels (name, profession, parent, nationality) that cripple the divine self.
more: In the Vox interview Athena lists what we take for the self: thoughts, which pass while I remain; emotions that turn from sorrow to joy; desires; our parents' 'musts'; the image we want to show. All of it is the non-self, and the light of intellect must pierce these layers to reach the protagonist at the centre.

label: Truth by subtraction
take: Truth, for her, is a subtractive process. You need to acquire nothing, because the soul already carries the seeds of eudaimonia, knowledge and freedom and is 'baptised in the light of wisdom'; you only remove what covers it. On the radio she pictures it as a flower opening petal by petal as we shed roles. In the 28 October talk every subtraction is a «No», which is why the national «No» stirs Greeks, though a «No» must then be completed by a «Yes».
more: Asked what self-knowledge made Athena cast off, the answer is 'everything': ways of living, diet, habits, identities, labels and roles, since one in love with truth, like any lover, will do everything. And when every title, role and expectation is gone, what remains is everything: the All.

label: Aletheia, unforgetting
take: She reads ἀλήθεια as alpha privative plus λήθη: truth is the lifting of forgetfulness. This fits Plato's teaching that knowledge is recollection, so knowing is activating what we already carry, not conquering something foreign, which she calls one of the most distinctive features of the Greek view. In the Pythagoras lesson she adds an anagram: ἀλήθεια and θήλεια, the female, so truth is always gestating and giving birth.

label: Touching truth
take: For the ancients, she says, philosophy's goal was to touch (ἐφάπτεσθαι) the truth experientially, not to master arguments. The touch is as tangible as touch, the heaviest sense, yet as dimensionless as Euclid's point. Since ἅπτω also means to kindle (think of a lighter, αναπτήρας), touching truth sets the whole being ablaze and rekindles the inner fire, contact with Heraclitus' ever-living fire.

label: Union with the Monad
take: Ἕνωσις with the Monad is Pythagoras' name for what others call yoga, 'union', or nirvana, and for her it is the aim of philosophy. It is not reaching something far away but realising, with mind, heart and body, that you and the cosmic ocean are already one. The final step of the Pythagorean school, ὁμοίωσις θεῷ, is the same awakening: my essence and the universe's essence are one.
more: With Plotinus, Socrates and the Presocratics Athena names ἕνωσις as the aim, and stresses that union is not noetic like knowledge: to know, a subject must stand before an object, while in union that division collapses. Hence Plotinus' line that the seer was one with the seen, 'not a vision but a union', and why the ancients called it mystery.

label: Work and action
take: Awakening must become work. After 'make music' comes 'and work': like the freed prisoner who goes back down, the realised one builds the insight into a way of life, which is why the highest Pythagorean initiation was political. She glosses ἔργον as ἔρωτος γόνος, offspring of eros. In the Ares lesson all work and industriousness run on Arean energy, 'the moment I stand up', and truth not expressed in action is incomplete truth.

label: The Golden Verses
take: She describes the Golden Verses as 72 verses taught for a thousand years as the first lesson of the Platonic school, to be listened to as a vibration, not only as information. She reads their last lines as 'if' you leave the body, not 'when': leaving the body at death is not liberation, dropping the illusion that you are the body is. Their promise, 'an immortal god, no longer mortal', means you do not become immortal; you realise you always were.

label: Immortality
take: She separates two immortalities. The soul's immortality 'we already have'. The hero's immortality is a state of consciousness: defying death means not caring for one's own hide, so one dis-identifies from the ego, becomes one with the all, and since the all always is, how could one die? She reads βροτός, mortal, as 'eaten' (as in 'this problem is eating me'), so ἄμβροτος is the un-consumed, imperishable.

label: What is a Hellene
take: For her 'Hellene' is a level of the soul, not an ethnicity or a seed asleep in the DNA: an existential, cultural and spiritual achievement. She reads the name through 'Ἑλ', which she takes as spiritual light, so a Hellene is one who tunes his mind to that light, and since light knows no borders a Hellene cannot look after his own interest alone. Many Greeks, she says, are Hellenes in potential (ἐν δυνάμει) but not in actuality (ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ); in 1940 they were Hellenes in actuality.

label: Ancient as a quality
take: To fulfil the heritage, she says, we must become ancients ourselves, with no regressive intent. 'Ancient' is not a date but a quality: a being's position toward the ἀρχαί, the value principles, and toward the first ἀρχή, which some call God, others the first cause (πρωταίτιον), and our philosophers the Good.

label: The «No» and the «Yes»
take: She reads the «No» of 28 October 1940 as a philosophical lesson. Every subtraction on the path is a «No», said first within, which is why the national «No» stirs every Greek. But a «No» without a «Yes» is lame: a reaction stays locked to the action it opposes and carries the seeds of its perpetuation. The «Yes» is cultivation, the soil, water and pruning that let the seed of «No» sprout, and the two must cycle forever.

label: As above, so below
take: The second principle of Hellenism in her 28 October talk: what is above is like what is below, and what is within is like what is without, so there is continuity across all scales. She says it was in a sense given by the Greeks to the Egyptians and engraved on an emerald tablet, which she offers as her account. In Plato it becomes the mirroring of soul and polity, and in the Ares lesson the same law makes the force behind outer law a model for the soul.

label: Political eros
take: Against the modern foundation of politics on fear, she proposes the ancient one: political eros. It carries a positive sign of hope and love, and it is the summit of Diotima's ascent, an eros that rises beyond a beautiful body and soul to embrace the whole city: its nature, trees, buildings, citizens, institutions and laws. Since eros is activated by the καλόν, we must make ourselves lovable: be the change.

Hidden in the word ἐλευθερία

label: Cultivation
take: The word 'cultivation' is used for only two human activities, she notes: tilling the earth and tending the soul, so soul and earth are strangely identified. The soul needs good seed, good soil and continuous care in rhythm with nature's turns, as good farmers sow by the stars. Virtues make the soul gentle and fertile so it can receive the seed of spirit, and the «Yes» that completes the «No» is exactly this cultivation, with Demeter's help.

label: The three parts of the soul
take: She uses Plato's three parts of the soul in four talks: the desiring part, the spirited part, which she equates with the heart and emotions, and the reasoning part. Studying them is the first, valid stage of self-knowledge and an 'extremely therapeutic' practice of observation. But they are powers of the soul, not the soul: as the melody is not the kithara, the maker is not the made. Politically, when desire takes the reins, a people's regime turns tyrannical.

label: Acceptance and the ἔστω
take: For hard times she offers a mathematician's tool. As a proof starts from 'ἔστω', 'let it be so', one can take as a working hypothesis that everything is perfect and just and must happen for some reason, since from partway up the mountain we cannot see all the folds. Saying 'let it be' is acceptance, an attitude of mind and heart; because the ego is a form of resistance, each acceptance opens us to the Whole.
more: In the Vox interview Athena separates acceptance from tolerance and from resignation. Accepting while boiling inside is not acceptance: ἀποδοχή holds δέχομαι, to receive, to make room, and to forgive (συγχωρώ) and give something room near you is already love. To accept is to light a thing with understanding, to put oneself in the other's place and to embrace it with love; then, no longer entangled, one has the strength to act with discernment, even to leave. Fighting something keeps it close, as Ares and Aphrodite are a couple.

label: Gratitude and thanksgiving
take: She ends her lessons with gratitude. Εὐγνωμοσύνη contains γνώμων, a gauge: it is the measure that immediately activates the εὖ, the good and divine nature. It is a heart virtue that aligns the spirited part with the soul's purpose and 'leads the soul' toward its entelechy. Εὐχαριστία, from εὖ and χάρις, activates grace, the touch of the Three Graces or the right conjuncture, the incalculable factor that, with our own effort, completes eudaimonia.

label: Mantic knowing
take: Μαντική for her is not laurel-chewing or tripods but unmediated knowledge, reached in inner silence rather than by reading, being told or proving. It comes from divine μανία, which she reads as the sacred marriage of heart and nous, not madness. It is Apollo's second power (ἁπλοῦς): removing the many judgements reveals a simple truth, and 'each of us is a seer'. The great ideas of Einstein, Planck, Heisenberg and Tesla came this way, in flashes, with proofs later.

label: Plutarch
take: In On the E at Delphi Plutarch gives the five cult names of Apollo, learned from his teacher Ammonius, each matched to the seeker's condition; she reads them as five steps of awakening. He also treats Apollo and Dionysus as one, two states of the universe: the One becoming many and the many returning in a luminous, non-material fire. She departs from him in one place: he groups Delios and Phanaios together, while she makes them two separate steps.
more: Plutarch, philosopher and priest at Delphi, is Athena's witness that 'know thyself' was not given by a human but by Apollo himself, the light itself, which is why it was written on his temple as the god's own precept.

label: Plato's Cratylus
take: In the Cratylus Socrates gives four etymologies of Apollo's name matching his four powers: medicine (ἀπολούων), mantic (ἁπλοῦς), archery (ἀεὶ βάλλων) and music (ὁμοπολῶν). She uses them as the four passages between Plutarch's five names, since five steps have four intervals. She also takes from it the principle that letters can interchange and similar words share meaning, which licenses her wordplay.
more: Athena thinks everyone should read the Cratylus, because it gives the etymological keys of Greek, keys that have little or nothing to do with today's prevailing linguistics. To define love Athena uses 'a Platonic key': ἀγάπη from ἄγω and ἅπαν.

label: Health and healing
take: Apollo's first power is healing: father of Asclepius, he heals through light and pure vision. Greek medicine is holistic, illness starting in spirit or nous, then soul, then body; illness is complication and health is simplicity and a mean, with the noetic idea as the stable centre. In the eros talk, living in the flow of eros gives ῥῶσις, vigour, and with Socrates health is inner peace while illness is an inner civil war. Healing begins with the will to change.

label: Steady will
take: Healing starts with ρ, the intention and will to change: 'you must want to change', otherwise nothing moves. At the archer's step (ἀεὶ βάλλων) the will stops changing and holds one target; every traveller must choose one direction, vice or virtue, and carry it through, avoiding πολυπραγμοσύνη. Stabilising flashes of awakening into a way of life needs this steady will, like a diamond made of one element.

label: The ennead
take: Four etymologies plus five names make nine keys, and she reads the ennead as νέα ἑνάς, 'the new one'. It names the new unity that appears when Apollo, having gone beyond the poles, harmonises the many again. She ties this reading to the Pythagoreans.

label: Dialogue
take: At the fifth step, Leschenorios, Plutarch's seekers 'are active and enjoy using dialogue and philosophising with one another'. The λέσχη (from λέγω) was the place where initiates gathered, there was one at Delphi, and 'we are a lesche'. Shared dialogue is how a community lives devoted to knowledge, truth and the common good, as in the ancient philosophical schools.

Shared life becomes a feast.

label: Peace
take: She derives εἰρήνη from εἴρω, to join, the same root she finds in ἔρως, so 'peace and eros are two sides of the same coin'. Health is a form of inner peace and illness an inner civil war (στάσις), in the psyche and in society alike. Apollo's archery is 'a war of peace, of light' that in the end is not war: wildness touching a focused will is tamed.

talks.note: εἰρήνη from εἴρω, like ἔρως.
Peace and eros, two sides of one coin.
A war of peace, which is not war.

links.why: Same root, two sides of one coin.
Health is inner peace.
Both hold things together in one.
The archer wages a war of peace.
A focused will tames wildness.

label: Aphrodite
take: She recalls the two Aphrodites of Greek tradition: Οὐρανία, eros 'from here upward' through pure emotion and spirit, and Πάνδημος, eros approached in a lustful, bodily way. She uses the pair to suggest that societies promote different qualities of eros and could be studied that way.
more: Athena pairs Aphrodite with Ares: love and war are a couple and in a sense the same thing, since fighting is a way of holding close. Wrestlers on vases, or Heracles with the Nemean lion, look as if they embrace.

talks.note: Societies promote different kinds of eros.
Heavenly and common Aphrodite.
With Ares, a couple: fighting is a kind of embrace.

links.why: Two qualities of eros.
A society's Aphrodite reveals its health.
Pandemos is the bodily, lustful approach.
War too is an embrace, as the wrestlers on the vases show.

label: Silence
take: Mantic, unmediated knowledge is reached in inner silence. Without analysing, one lets an answer or awareness appear and trusts the intuition the heart speaks first, then the mind.

talks.note: Listen in silence for unmediated answers.

links.why: Mantic knowledge is heard in silence.
Meditation empties the mind of content.

label: The divided line
take: She reads the Line as the ordering of what the Sun taught: five objects of seeing or thinking and five modes of consciousness, from conjecture and opinion inside the cave, through knowledge of concepts and of numbers above it, to union with the Good at its top. She stresses that she decodes these five from the text rather than adding them, and that they match Plato's five levels of being, the five constitutions and the Pythagorean pentagram. The line is drawn in the mean and extreme ratio, φ.

talks.note: The Line sets in order what the Sun taught, in the mean and extreme ratio.
Five objects and five modes; she decodes rather than adds them.
Above a point on the line one leaves the cave for conscious νόησις.
Conjecture, opinion, knowledge (ideas, mathematics) and awakening as union.

links.why: The line is constructed in φ.
Its lowest mode is conjecture.
Its second mode is opinion and conviction.
The lower part of the line is the cave.
Its top is the sun of the Good.
The five modes of knowing match five levels of being.
Five is the Pythagorean rhythm of justice and the pentagram.

label: The golden ratio φ
take: The Line is constructed in the mean and extreme ratio, a formulation of φ, which she calls 'the rhythm of harmony', found in the Acropolis, flowers, shells, galaxies and the human body. Because every level relates to every higher one by the same ratio, φ is 'the magic key of justice', the harmony of all levels.

talks.note: Under the similes lies a geometry, the geometry of φ.
Divide a segment, then each part again, in the same ratio.
φ structures the Acropolis, flowers, the body, shells and galaxies.
φ is the magic key of justice, the harmony of all levels.

links.why: φ is the key of justice as harmony of levels.
φ is the rhythm of harmony.
The line is drawn in this ratio.
Esoteric knowledge encoded in mathematics.

label: Conjecture (eikasia)
take: The lowest mode of mind, when intellection turns to images and shadows. She reads the shadows psychologically: the shadows of the personality, traumas and the projections we cast on others, as when a partner's morning frown becomes 'he doesn't love me'. This is where psychology and Jung's shadow work come in.

talks.note: Turned to images and shadows, the mind forms conjectures and projections.
The shadows are the personality's shadows, traumas and projections.
Seeing a sullen husband and concluding 'he doesn't love me' is projection.
In conjecture one is lost in the mass: what others say and believe.

links.why: It is the lowest segment of the line.
The next mode up is opinion.
Noticing when I conjecture is the first practice.
Projections come from the personality and its wounds.
The shadows on the wall.

label: Opinion and conviction
take: When we turn to sensible objects we form opinions, beliefs and views, the 'my view and your view' prized in democracy, and she places them inside the cave, in what she calls the deep cave. They rest on the belief 'I am the body and others are bodies'. A conviction is an opinion clothed in emotion, which is why even science, studied only materialistically, can turn into dogma and fanaticism, as Kuhn saw with paradigms.

talks.note: Views so prized in democracy are inside the cave.
They rest on the conviction that I am the body and you are a body.
This part of the line is the deep cave.
A conviction is an opinion clothed in emotion.
Kuhn: communities resist paradigm change from emotional investment.

links.why: Opinion is the mode just above conjecture.
Opinions rest on identifying with the body.
Materialist science becomes conviction and dogma.
Most people run through the wonder-worker: 'I have a view and believe it'.
Watching when I hold a view is how one starts to leave the cave.
Changing a conviction threatens the knower's role.

label: The wonder-workers
take: Outwardly they are all who build a mass reality: television, the news, the models people are told to believe. But while everyone wants to catch the outer wonder-workers, she turns inward: the true wonder-worker is the nous itself. Most people, she says with Plato, run through the wonder-worker: 'I have a view and I believe it.'

talks.note: Today's spiritual scene is full of wonder-mongering, as in Plato.
Governments, propagandists and religions are wonder-workers too, but the inner one matters.
They are all who take part in constructing a mass reality.
Most people function through the wonder-worker.

links.why: The one wonder-worker is the mind.
They supply the opinions people believe.
They carry the figures whose shadows the prisoners see.
Spiritual wonder-mongering renovates the cave.
Contact with them is a stage of liberation.

label: The Horai and the soul's ripe hour
take: Her own gate out of the cave is the ripeness of the soul: the hour has come, as chamomile springs up in spring once all the conditions are met. Since the talk is about justice, she notes that the Horai are the first daughters of Zeus by Themis, goddess of justice, and that their sisters the Graces name the same moment as grace. She says she is writing a treatise on the Horai.

talks.note: Ripeness of the soul: something inside has ripened, its hour has come.
The Horai are daughters of Zeus and Themis; she is writing a treatise on them.
The hour is also called grace; the Graces are sisters of the Horai.

links.why: The ripe hour is the sudden moment of release.
The Horai are daughters of Themis, goddess of justice.
They are Zeus's first daughters by Themis.
The great calling can also come as Eros.
It is the soul's own ripening.

label: Illusion and interpretation
take: She refuses to call life an illusion, since then the Good would have created something false; illusion is produced by interpretation, the way our nous works. The greatest illusion of the spiritual scene is 'the awakened subject'. After the return she says even illusion is awakening that forgets itself.

talks.note: Speaking of the awakened subject is one of the greatest illusions.
It is not that life is an illusion; the Good does not create something false.
Illusion is created by interpretation; the error is the interpretation (partly reconstructed).
Even illusion is awakening that forgets itself.

links.why: The 'awakened one' is itself an illusion.
The belief 'I am this body, personality, role' does not hold.
The Good does not create anything false.
Illusion comes from how the mind interprets.
On return, illusion is seen as forgetful awakening.
Interpretations and projections are the shadows.

label: The new spiritual cave
take: Her name for the 'renovation of the cave' produced by today's inflation of spiritual terms: awakening approached materialistically, what other traditions call spiritual materialism, with wonder-mongering and misinformation. Identities such as 'the awakened one', or a spirituality fenced by race, are further versions of it.

talks.note: Interest in awakening brings a terminological and ideational inflation.
She calls it the new spiritual cave, a renovation of the cave.
Other traditions speak of spiritual materialism.
Body-centred categories in spirituality can become another cave.

links.why: It is the cave renovated in spiritual dress.
Awakening is its main inflated term.
It is full of wonder-mongering.
A racially fenced Greek spirituality is another cave.
'The awakened one' is a new identity.

label: Participation (methexis)
take: Her word for the final stage of the Line and of the ascent: participation in, or union with, the One, the Good, after one has already come to know ideas and numbers. She reads the Symposium's formless final spectacle as this μέθεξις. With Plotinus she adds that in the end 'there was not even union', since one was always the One.

talks.note: The Symposium's spectacle without form or colour is μέθεξις with the One.
The last mode of the line: μέθεξις with the monad, the One.
The ascent must culminate in absolute μέθεξις with the sun of the Good.

links.why: It is participation in the One.
Its object is the sun of the Good.
It is the top of the line.
Beholding becomes union.
In the end there was not even union.

label: Observing the mind
take: What is now called mindfulness, she says, is the path of self-knowledge: recognising at each moment how your mind works, noticing when you conjecture and when you simply hold an opinion and believe it. Learning to function without the mediation of views, dogmas and convictions is where one begins to leave the cave. Her book in progress, based on her course on the cave, focuses on this.

talks.note: This is what is called mindfulness, the focus of her book.
Notice each moment when you conjecture and when you hold a view.
Functioning without views and dogmas, we begin to leave the cave.
Create a space between what I think and the I who observes it.

links.why: It watches how the nous works.
It catches conjectures and projections.
It catches opinions believed without examination.
It is her practice drawn from sophia.
It is the path of self-knowledge.
It is how one starts to leave the cave.

label: Hermes
take: Those freed who go back into the cave to help lead her to the epithet ψυχοπομπός, guide of souls, belonging to Hermes, 'the symbol of the teacher who unites the two worlds'. With his caduceus he leads Persephone back to Demeter in spring. Crossing the dark valley, one needs a good psychopomp.
more: In the Vox interview Athena calls Hermes the god of thought: with winged sandals and the winged petasos he runs here and there and cannot be caught, as thoughts pass while the self remains.

talks.note: With a good psychopomp one crosses the valley of darkness into light (probably hers).
Hermes the psychopomp is the symbol of the teacher who unites two worlds.
He holds the caduceus and leads Persephone back to Demeter in spring.
Hermes is the god of thought: winged, running, never caught.

links.why: The returning teacher is a psychopomp.
He is the symbol of the teacher.
He unites the world inside and outside the cave.
Hermes is thought, which runs off while the self remains.

label: Reincarnation
take: Taking up the host's point that souls may have lived in East and West, she says the passer-by of another ethnicity could be Aristotle reborn, so racial distinctions miss the soul. She notes that Book X of the Republic teaches metempsychosis, and mocks the academic view that Plato 'got tired' and threw in the myth of Er.

talks.note: The host raises Plato's metempsychosis: souls cross East and West.
Her example: the passer-by may be Aristotle, reincarnated.
Book X tells how reincarnation and metempsychosis take place.
Academics said Plato threw in the myth of Er.

links.why: Racial identity ignores the travelling soul.
A Greek today may have been Eastern before.
Book X teaches it.
Academics dismiss this part of Plato.

label: Enlightenment
take: She uses φώτισις nearly interchangeably with awakening for the completion at the top of the line. Her criterion: as long as you say 'I am the enlightened one', it is not complete. The true state is Οὖτις, Odysseus's 'Nobody', which Plotinus calls silence and Buddhists the luminous void.

talks.note: The last mode of the line is awakening, enlightenment, the completion.
'I am the enlightened one' means it is not complete.
It is pure consciousness, Odysseus's Nobody, the nobody-the-all.

links.why: Used almost as a synonym.
An enlightened identity means it is incomplete.
Odysseus as Οὖτις, Nobody.
Plotinus calls the completed state silence.
Buddhists call it the luminous void.

label: The heroic path
take: In Athena's reading the hero is not a romantic figure but a stage in the evolution of consciousness, as Plato and later Platonism describe it. Human consciousness turns in the cycle of days; then suddenly something pushes, and a spark of eros lights, eros in the ontological sense: 'this does not fill me, I want my freedom'. From there begin the labours (ἆθλοι) needed to find who one is at one's centre, like Theseus going to the heart of the labyrinth. Ἥρως comes from ἔρως, so without eros there is no heroic path.
more: Self-knowledge is a marathon that never stops, and Athena calls it athletics: ἀθλητισμός comes from ἆθλος. So every temple had a stadium or gymnasium beside it (at Delphi the stadium stands above the temple of Apollo, and the gymnasium near Athena Pronaia is larger than the temple), and the ancient schools began with the body: train the soul as you train the body. The hero must go against the currents of illusion set by upbringing, inner programming, fate (εἱμαρμένη) or society, with the strength (σθένος) of Athena, goddess of all heroes. After the ἆθλος comes the ἔπαθλον: completion, fullness, peace and love.

talks.note: Self-knowledge is athletics, and ἥρως comes from ἔρως.
The heroic as a stage of human consciousness, after Plato.
A spark of eros: from human to heroic consciousness.
A stadium or gymnasium beside every temple.
Athena, goddess of heroes, guides them against the currents.
After the labour, the prize: fullness, peace, love.

links.why: Ἥρως comes from ἔρως: without eros there is no heroic path.
Suddenly something pushes and a spark of eros lights.
Athena guides every hero: Theseus, Odysseus, Heracles.
The hero needs the strength to go against the current.
Plato treats the heroic as a stage of human consciousness.
Theseus must reach the centre of the labyrinth and kill the Minotaur, the ego.
The hero goes against currents of illusion from upbringing, programming, fate or society.
Self-knowledge is a marathon, an ἆθλος for a hero.
At Delphi a stadium stands above the temple: training beside every temple.
After the ἆθλος comes the prize: fullness, peace and love.

label: One's own work
take: To young people asking what to study and to adults whose fire has gone out, Athena gives the same answer: come to your centre, listen to your heart and ask what you love to do. The ancients held that every soul is born with a mission, its οἰκεῖον ἔργον, the work closest and warmest to its heart; doing what is one's own is οἰκειοπραγία. Fulfil it and you feel full and εὐδαίμων. Athena's two criteria: you burn with zeal for it, and while doing it you lose the sense of time, because love works in eternity.
more: Athena calls those who have lost it σβηστοί, extinguished people: the flame of youth has gone out, swallowed by daily life, and they say their life does not fill them and they live as if imprisoned. To one who loves music but works as a marketing director Athena's advice is simple: become a musician. Follow love, and love will set you free.

talks.note: Do what you love: set love as the central axis of life.
Extinguished people whose fire has gone out.
Every soul is born to fulfil its own work.
Two criteria: zeal, and losing the sense of time.
Follow love, and love will set you free.

links.why: Do what you love: love shows each soul its own work.
Fulfilling one's own work makes one full and εὐδαίμων.
In one's own work one loses the sense of time.
Follow love, and love will set you free.
To find it, come to your centre and listen to your heart.

label: Faith (pistis)
take: For Athena faith is not the opposite of knowledge but a necessary step towards it, a 'scientific stage' found in the theory of knowledge of Plato's Republic: the interval between ignorance and knowledge. To believe (πιστεύω) is to give credit (πίστωση) that something may be so, as a scientist believes a new theory possible before shutting himself in the lab to prove it; that is why πίστη sits inside the word ἐπιστήμη. Faith in the good is the voice of Mnemosyne in us, an inner knowing that our nature, like the nature of the universe, is the Good.
more: At the summit faith ends. In union, which Plotinus calls not a vision but a union, one no longer believes in God or the Good but is its witness and lives it. Because this goes beyond discursive knowing it cannot be put in terms of knowledge: there is the faith that leads, and its fruit, the experience itself.

talks.note: Faith is a necessary step of knowing, a scientific stage.
Between ignorance and knowledge, in Plato's theory of knowledge.
To believe is to give credit, as a scientist does before the proof.
Faith in the good is Mnemosyne's voice within.
At union faith gives way to witnessing.

links.why: Πίστη sits inside ἐπιστήμη: the scientist believes before proving.
Faith is the interval between ignorance and knowledge.
The Republic's theory of knowledge holds faith as a stage.
Faith in the good is the voice of Mnemosyne within us.
It believes because it already knows our nature is the Good.
At union faith ends: you witness and live it.
